alcohol-units-and-low-risk-drinking.name: Alcohol units: the UK low-risk drinking advice
alcohol-units-and-low-risk-drinking.summary: The UK Chief Medical Officers advise adults not to regularly drink more than 14 units a week, spread over three days or more.
keyPoints: The UK Chief Medical Officers advise that adults should not regularly drink more than 14 units of alcohol a week.
Their guidance says there is no completely safe level of regular drinking, because no level of regular consumption improves health.
One unit is 10 millilitres, or 8 grams, of pure alcohol, and the strength printed on a label as ABV can be used to work out units.
For anyone who is pregnant or could become pregnant, the Chief Medical Officers advise that the safest approach is not to drink alcohol at all.

body.heading: What is the UK low-risk drinking advice?
body.body: The UK Chief Medical Officers advise that, to keep the risk of harm from alcohol low, adults should not regularly drink more than 14 units a week. For someone who drinks as much as 14 units, the advice is to spread it evenly over three days or more. The guidance also says there is no definitively safe lower limit, because no level of regular drinking improves health. Some older leaflets still quote daily limits, but the weekly figure is the one in the current guidance.

body.heading: What is an alcohol unit?
body.body: One unit is 10 millilitres of pure alcohol, which is 8 grams. The strength of a drink is shown on the label as alcohol by volume, or ABV. Units can be worked out by multiplying the volume in millilitres by the ABV percentage and dividing by 1,000. Using that method, a pint of strong lager at 5.2% ABV comes to about three units. As a guide, 14 units is about six pints of average-strength beer or six medium glasses of average-strength wine.

body.heading: What does drinking above the guidance do to health?
body.body: The Chief Medical Officers' guidance links regular drinking above the low-risk level with a range of long-term conditions, including seven types of cancer, heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes and mental health problems. It also names accidents and injuries, alcohol poisoning and harm from violence or abuse among the short-term risks. Drinking a large amount in a short time carries a particular risk of alcohol poisoning. Mouth cancers are more common among people who drink, and the risk is higher still when drinking is combined with smoking or any form of tobacco.

body.heading: Does keeping to 14 units remove the risk?
body.body: The 2016 review behind the guidance estimated that the lifetime risk of dying from an alcohol-related condition is around 1 per cent, or a little under, for people drinking at the low-risk level. Heavier drinking raises the risk further. The guidance is therefore described as a way to keep risk low, not to remove it.

body.heading: Who is advised not to drink at all?
body.body: For anyone who is pregnant or thinks they could become pregnant, the Chief Medical Officers advise that the safest approach is not to drink alcohol at all.

body.heading: When might someone need support with drinking?
body.body: Signs listed as a reason to seek support include drinking more over time, struggling to cut down, poor sleep, thinking ahead to the next drink, risky behaviour and concern from other people.

body.heading: How does the NHS suggest cutting down?
body.body: The NHS Better Health site points people to their local alcohol support service, or to Drinkline on 0300 123 1110, which it describes as free, confidential help for anyone concerned about their own or someone else's drinking. It also offers the NHS Drink Free Days app for setting a weekly unit target. NHS pages describe a drinks diary as a way to see how much is being drunk, in which situations, and how cutting down could start. Having several alcohol-free days each week is another suggestion, as are eating before drinking, choosing lower-strength drinks and diluting drinks.

body.heading: What treatment exists for alcohol dependence?
body.body: The NHS says treatment for alcohol use disorder is available from a GP or a specialist alcohol service. Options it lists include counselling, self-help groups, talking therapies such as CBT, and medicines. Alcoholics Anonymous, Al-Anon UK and SMART Recovery are named as support groups. The NHS says a person who is not ready to stop, or who only wants to cut down, will be supported to reduce drinking to a safer level. A Scottish NHS leaflet for heavier drinkers warns against stopping suddenly, because withdrawal symptoms can follow, and says symptoms such as shakes or sweats call for NHS 111 or urgent medical attention.

asthma-and-copd-how-they-differ.name: Asthma and COPD: how they differ
asthma-and-copd-how-they-differ.headline: Asthma and COPD: how they differ in cause, symptoms and treatment
asthma-and-copd-how-they-differ.summary: Asthma causes variable, reversible airway narrowing that often starts young; COPD is mostly smoking-related and worsens over time.
keyPoints: Asthma symptoms come and go and vary between people, while COPD symptoms are usually more persistent and tend to worsen over time.
The main cause of COPD is smoking, though it can affect people who have never smoked.
Clinicians use history, age at onset and breathing tests such as spirometry to tell the two apart.
Asthma is mainly treated with inhalers; COPD cannot be reversed, but treatment and stopping smoking can slow it.
A reliever inhaler that stops working during an attack is an emergency: the NHS says to call 999.

body.heading: What is asthma?
body.body:
Asthma is a common long-term condition that affects the airways. The NHS says the main symptoms are wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath and a tight chest, and that they often come and go.

Symptoms range from mild to severe, and they can be set off by triggers such as allergies, cold air, exercise and infections. The NHS says the exact cause of asthma is not fully understood, but allergies, a family history of asthma or allergies, and early-life exposure to air pollution or cigarette smoke are among the factors linked with it.

body.heading: What is COPD?
body.body:
COPD, short for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, is the name for a group of lung conditions that cause breathing difficulties. It includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis.

The NHS says the main cause is smoking, although it can sometimes affect people who have never smoked. Typical symptoms are breathlessness on exertion, a persistent chesty cough with phlegm, frequent chest infections and wheeze. They tend to get worse over time.

body.heading: How do doctors tell them apart?
body.body:
The two conditions can look alike, and some people have both. NICE advises using features from the person's history to help tell them apart: smoking history, the age when symptoms began, whether breathlessness is persistent and progressive or variable, and whether symptoms vary from day to day or wake the person at night.

Breathing tests help. Spirometry measures how much air a person can blow out and how fast, and it is used for both conditions. The site's spirometry page explains the test, and the laboratory or clinic report shows the reference values used.

Because symptoms vary and breathing problems have more than one cause, the NHS notes that diagnosing asthma can take time.

body.heading: How are the two treated?
body.body:
Asthma has no cure, but the NHS says the main treatment is medicine breathed in through an inhaler, which works well for most people. Reliever inhalers ease symptoms when they occur, and preventer inhalers are used regularly to reduce them. An asthma action plan is usually agreed with a doctor or asthma nurse.

COPD cannot be reversed, but its progression can be slowed, and stopping smoking is one of the most effective steps. Treatment mainly relieves symptoms, with inhalers, and pulmonary rehabilitation may help people become more active.

body.heading: When is breathlessness an emergency?
body.body:
Asthma attacks can be life-threatening. The NHS says urgent medical help is needed if symptoms get worse or if the reliever inhaler stops working, and the route for that is 999.

For COPD, sudden worsening breathlessness is also a reason to seek urgent help. NHS 111 can advise when it is unclear how serious a flare-up is.

A GP appointment is the route for new or persistent breathing symptoms, so that the cause can be found.

body.heading: What helps people living with either condition?
body.body:
Both conditions are reviewed regularly by a GP or nurse. Not smoking, and avoiding known triggers for asthma, are common themes in NHS advice.

Vaccinations against flu and some other infections are often offered to people with long-term lung conditions, because chest infections can cause flare-ups. The care team can explain what applies in each case.

bleeding-after-menopause-and-between-per.name: Bleeding after menopause or between periods
bleeding-after-menopause-and-between-per.headline: Vaginal bleeding after the menopause or between periods: causes and next steps
bleeding-after-menopause-and-between-per.summary: Any vaginal bleeding after the menopause should be checked by a GP. It is often caused by something other than cancer, but womb cancer is one possible cause.
keyPoints: NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP for any bleeding after the menopause, even a small amount of blood, spotting or pink or brown discharge.
The NHS lists bleeding or spotting after the menopause as a main symptom of womb cancer, but it has other, more common causes.
NHS inform says anyone with vaginal bleeding after the menopause is referred urgently, within two weeks.
A scan of the womb lining is often the first test, and a small sample of the lining may follow.

body.heading: What counts as bleeding after the menopause?
body.body: Bleeding after the menopause means vaginal bleeding once periods have stopped, and the NHS lists it among the main symptoms of womb cancer. NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP even if the amount is small, or if it is spotting or pink or brown discharge.

body.heading: Does it mean cancer?
body.body: Bleeding has many possible causes, and cancer is a less common one. The causes NHS 111 Wales lists include thinning of the vaginal or womb lining from lower oestrogen, benign polyps and a thickened womb lining. Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) can also be linked with bleeding. The NHS advises not waiting to contact a GP, because finding womb cancer early can make it easier to treat.

body.heading: What about bleeding between periods?
body.body: The NHS lists bleeding between periods, unusually heavy periods and a change in vaginal discharge as other possible signs of womb cancer. NHS advice on heavy periods and pelvic pain also lists bleeding between periods or after sex as a reason to see a GP.

body.heading: How quickly will someone be seen?
body.body: NHS inform says that a person with vaginal bleeding after the menopause is referred urgently, to be seen within two weeks. Referral rules can differ between the UK nations, so the exact pathway depends on where the person lives.

body.heading: What tests might be offered?
body.body: The first test is usually a transvaginal ultrasound scan, which measures the thickness of the womb lining. A small sample of the womb lining (biopsy) may follow, and some clinics use hysteroscopy, a look inside the womb with a thin camera. Treatment depends on the cause; for thinning of the vaginal lining it can include local oestrogen cream.

blood-in-urine-causes-and-what-happens-n.name: Blood in urine: causes and what happens next
blood-in-urine-causes-and-what-happens-n.headline: Blood in your urine: common causes and why the NHS wants it checked
blood-in-urine-causes-and-what-happens-n.summary: Blood in the urine is not usually serious, but the NHS advises seeing a GP every time, even if the amount is small, because cancer is one possible cause.
keyPoints: The NHS says blood in the urine is not usually serious, but it is important to get medical help.
Urinary tract infections, kidney stones and an enlarged prostate are the usual causes the NHS lists.
The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or contacting NHS 111 for blood in the pee, even if there is only a little or it is the first time.
Beetroot, some medicines, bleeding from the back passage or a period can make urine look pink or red.

body.heading: What does blood in urine look like?
body.body: Blood in the urine may look bright pink, red or dark brown. Beetroot, some medicines, bleeding from the back passage or a period can make urine look pink or red, so these do not always mean blood in the urine. The NHS says to get checked even if you are unsure whether it is blood.

body.heading: What are the common causes?
body.body: The NHS lists urinary tract infections, kidney stones and an enlarged prostate as the usual causes. The other symptoms that come with each of these can give a clue to the cause. Kidney inflammation and blood-thinning medicines are also named as possible causes.

body.heading: Could it be cancer?
body.body: Cancers of the bladder, kidney or prostate are on the NHS list of possible causes, which is why the NHS stresses that blood in the urine must be checked. Blood in the urine is the most common symptom of bladder cancer. The NHS notes that blood in the urine is not usually a sign of anything serious.

body.heading: When should you get help?
body.body: The NHS says to see a GP about blood in the urine even if the amount is small. The NHS bladder cancer page says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 for blood in the pee, even with no other symptoms, if it is the first time, if there is only a little, or if you are not sure it is blood. The NHS advises against trying to diagnose the cause yourself.

body.heading: What will a GP do?
body.body: A GP will ask about symptoms and may examine the person. A urine sample or blood test may be requested, antibiotics may be prescribed for a suspected infection, or a referral to a specialist may be made. At a specialist clinic, the checks can include an ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder and a look inside the bladder with a thin flexible camera.

blood-pressure-at-home-how-it-works.name: Home blood pressure checks: how they work
blood-pressure-at-home-how-it-works.summary: The NHS says people can buy a monitor to check blood pressure at home, using an upper arm cuff, sitting relaxed and avoiding caffeine and smoking first.
keyPoints: High blood pressure does not usually cause symptoms, so measuring it is the way to find out.
Blood pressure is written as two numbers, the first higher than the second.
NHS-linked guidance recommends an upper arm monitor rather than a wrist or finger device.
A single high reading is usually not a cause for alarm, and a GP or nurse decides the schedule and target.

body.heading: What does a blood pressure check show?
body.body: The NHS says a blood pressure test can check whether blood pressure is too high or too low. High blood pressure does not usually have any symptoms, while low blood pressure can cause dizziness or fainting. Readings are given as two numbers with the first higher than the second; the top figure is the pressure as the heart pumps and the bottom is the lowest pressure between beats.

body.heading: Can people check at home?
body.body: The NHS says people can use their own device, and that a blood pressure machine can be bought for home use. NHS England has a programme of home blood pressure monitoring through GP practices. The NHS says blood pressure is usually considered high at a lower figure when checked at home than when checked by a healthcare professional.

body.heading: How is a home reading usually taken?
body.body: Local NHS guides recommend an automatic upper arm monitor with a cuff that fits snugly, and say that wrist and finger devices are not recommended. They describe sitting quietly for about five minutes with feet flat and the back supported, and avoiding caffeine, smoking, exercise and eating for about 30 minutes beforehand. Readings are usually taken twice in the morning and twice in the evening over about a week, with the average worked out afterwards. The guides advise taking readings before blood pressure tablets and leaving at least a minute between two readings. One guide recommends choosing a monitor validated by the British and Irish Hypertension Society.

body.heading: What happens next?
body.body: The NHS says the GP or nurse decides the schedule and the target for each person. One guide notes that a single high reading is usually not a cause for alarm and that it can be retaken later. Readings that are consistently high are a reason to contact the GP practice, according to one NHS integrated care board page, and very high readings with symptoms need same-day advice from NHS 111 or the GP practice.

bone-health-keeping-bones-strong.name: Bone health: what helps keep bones strong
bone-health-keeping-bones-strong.summary: NHS pages link bone health to weight-bearing exercise, calcium, vitamin D, not smoking and keeping alcohol low; inactivity raises osteoporosis risk.
keyPoints: NHS guidance treats weight-bearing and resistance exercise as the most useful activity for bone strength.
Calcium is important for bone health, and vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium.
Being inactive, being under or over weight, smoking and heavy drinking are listed as risk factors for weaker bones.
The NHS advises adults aged 65 and over to include strength and balance activities on at least two days a week.

body.heading: What helps keep bones strong?
body.body: NHS guidance treats weight-bearing and resistance exercise as the most useful activities for bone density. Running, skipping, dancing, aerobics and jumping are named as higher-impact examples that strengthen muscles, ligaments and joints. Swimming and cycling support general fitness but are not weight-bearing, so they do less for the bones. Being inactive makes muscles and bones lose strength, which raises the risk of osteoporosis, falls and fractures.

body.heading: What do calcium and vitamin D do?
body.body: The NHS says calcium is important for maintaining bone health. Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium, and the NHS osteoporosis page suggests a daily supplement containing 10 micrograms of vitamin D for people at risk. Sunlight helps too, but all adults are advised to consider a daily vitamin D supplement, particularly from October to March.

body.heading: What raises the risk of weaker bones?
body.body: Being underweight or overweight is listed as a risk for osteopenia, the stage of bone loss before osteoporosis, and for broken bones. Smoking and heavy drinking are also listed, and one source gives the low-risk alcohol guidance of less than 14 units a week. A high-salt diet is flagged in one source because sodium increases the calcium lost in urine.

body.heading: What changes after 65?
body.body: NHS guidance for people aged 65 and over advises activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least two days a week. It also advises about 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week, built up gradually from current levels. The NHS advises anyone diagnosed with osteoporosis to talk to a GP or specialist before starting a new exercise programme. A DEXA bone density scan is the standard test for bone loss.

breast-lump-what-happens-after-you-find-.name: Found a breast lump: what happens next
breast-lump-what-happens-after-you-find-.headline: Found a breast lump? Causes, the GP appointment and what the breast clinic does
breast-lump-what-happens-after-you-find-.summary: Most breast lumps are harmless, but the NHS advises seeing a GP about any new lump so it can be checked. A GP examines the breast and refers to a breast clinic if the cause is unclear.
keyPoints: The NHS says most breast lumps are harmless, with fibroadenomas and cysts among the common causes.
A GP appointment is advised for any new breast lump, even if it is painless.
If the GP is unsure of the cause, they refer to a hospital breast clinic.
Breast clinic checks usually combine an examination, an imaging scan and sometimes a biopsy.

body.heading: Are most breast lumps harmless?
body.body: The NHS says most breast lumps are not cancer. Common causes include fibroadenomas, which are solid benign lumps, and cysts, which are fluid-filled sacs. An injury to the breast can also cause a lump, and cancer is a possible but less common cause.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises contacting a GP about any lump in the breast or armpit. Changes to the nipple, dimpling of the skin and bloodstained discharge from the nipple are also reasons to be seen. A new lump is worth getting checked even if it is painless. The NHS page advises against trying to diagnose the cause yourself.

body.heading: What happens at the GP appointment?
body.body: The GP asks about symptoms, family history of breast or ovarian cancer and any past breast screening. The GP then examines the breasts. If the GP is not sure what is causing the lump, they refer the person to a breast clinic at a hospital.

body.heading: How is an urgent referral decided?
body.body: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, NICE guidance on suspected cancer sets out who should be offered an urgent referral to a breast clinic. The referral aims for a specialist appointment within two weeks. Scotland uses its own referral guidance, so the details can differ by nation.

body.heading: What does the breast clinic do?
body.body: Tests at a breast clinic usually include an examination of the breasts and an imaging scan, usually a mammogram or an ultrasound. Sometimes a biopsy is taken, in which a needle removes a small sample of cells from the lump. The tests are often done in the same visit, results are often given on the same day, and biopsy results can take about a week.

cardiovascular-service-framework-england.name: Heart disease and stroke framework for England
cardiovascular-service-framework-england.headline: Government and NHS England publish a 10-year framework on heart disease and stroke
cardiovascular-service-framework-england.summary: The government and NHS England have published a cardiovascular disease framework that aims to cut premature deaths from heart disease and stroke by a quarter within a decade.
keyPoints: The Department of Health and Social Care and NHS England published a cardiovascular disease modern service framework on 7 July 2026.
It sets a 10-year aim of cutting premature deaths from heart disease and stroke in England by a quarter.
The government describes 12 priorities for the first three years.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body: The government and NHS England say the framework is a 10-year strategic vision to reduce premature deaths from heart disease and stroke in England. It sets out 12 priorities for the next three years. The government says the priorities include finding people at risk of cardiovascular disease, blood pressure and cholesterol treatment targets, stroke care and rehabilitation. It also includes a partnership with Diabetes UK to raise public awareness of the link between type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: The government estimates that successful implementation could prevent between 1,600 and 2,400 premature deaths a year from heart disease and stroke in people under 75 in the first three years. It estimates this would rise to between 3,850 and 4,900 deaths a year after a decade. These are the government's projections, not results already achieved. The government describes the framework as part of a shift from reactive care towards prevention.

cholesterol-and-diet-what-the-nhs-says.name: High cholesterol: diet, tests and medicines
cholesterol-and-diet-what-the-nhs-says.summary: The NHS says cutting down on saturated fat can help lower cholesterol, and that medicines such as statins are considered when lifestyle changes are not enough.
keyPoints: High cholesterol means too much of a fatty substance called cholesterol in the blood, and it usually causes no symptoms.
The NHS advises cutting down on fatty food, especially saturated fat, and swapping to unsaturated fats.
Soluble fibre from foods such as oats, barley, beans and lentils is described as helping to lower cholesterol.
A blood test, sometimes called a lipid profile, measures cholesterol, and an NHS Health Check in England may offer it.

body.heading: What is cholesterol and why does it matter?
body.body: High cholesterol means having too much of a fatty substance called cholesterol in the blood. The body needs some cholesterol, but too much can narrow the arteries over time. HDL is often called good cholesterol because it helps clear excess cholesterol from the blood, while LDL is the main type of bad cholesterol and can build up in artery walls. High cholesterol usually causes no symptoms, which is why a blood test is used to find it.

body.heading: Who is more likely to have it?
body.body: Causes and risk factors listed by the NHS and the British Heart Foundation include eating a lot of fatty food, not being active enough, being overweight, smoking and drinking alcohol. It can also run in families, and the risk is higher for people over 50, men, people who have been through the menopause, and people of South Asian or sub-Saharan African origin.

body.heading: What does diet change?
body.body: The NHS advises cutting down on fatty food, especially food containing saturated fat. NHS and charity pages suggest unsaturated fats instead, such as oily fish, nuts, seeds and olive or rapeseed oil, and list butter, cream, hard cheese, cakes and biscuits among foods to limit. Soluble fibre from oats, barley, beans, pulses and lentils is described as helping to lower cholesterol. Plant sterols and stanols, added to some spreads and yoghurt drinks, can also help, although they are not suitable for everyone. A hospital trust leaflet says cholesterol in foods such as eggs has little effect on blood cholesterol compared with saturated fat.

body.heading: When are medicines considered?
body.body: The NHS says medicine may be needed if cholesterol has not gone down after changes to diet and lifestyle, or if a person is at high risk of a heart attack or stroke. Statins are the most common medicine for high cholesterol, and the NHS says people usually need to take them for life.

body.heading: How is cholesterol tested?
body.body: Testing is a blood test, sometimes called a lipid profile. In England it can be offered as part of an NHS Health Check for people aged 40 to 74 who do not already have cardiovascular disease. A GP may also suggest a test for someone with high blood pressure, diabetes, overweight, smoking or a family history of heart disease. Targets depend on age, other health conditions and heart risk, so the laboratory report and the clinician set what applies to each person.

dhsc-under-18-sales-ban-vapes-nicotine-p.name: Under-18 ban on vapes and nicotine in force
dhsc-under-18-sales-ban-vapes-nicotine-p.summary: New rules took effect on 29 October 2026 making it illegal to sell any vape or non-medicinal nicotine product to anyone under 18, according to a Department of Health and Social Care explainer.
keyPoints: The Department of Health and Social Care published its explainer on 29 October 2026, the day the rules took effect.
Selling any vaping product or non-medicinal nicotine product to under-18s is illegal, online or in shop.
Adults who buy these products for under-18s now commit an offence.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
The Department of Health and Social Care says it is illegal to sell any vaping product or non-medicinal nicotine product to anyone under 18, whether online or in a shop. The ban now covers nicotine-free vapes, which were not covered before, and tobacco-free nicotine pouches.

Buying these products for someone under 18, known as proxy purchasing, is now an offence.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
The rules restrict free giveaways and substantial discounts used to promote sales and ban most vending-machine sales. Enforcement authorities in England and Wales can issue £200 fixed penalty notices. Legal vaping products remain available to adults.

Separate tobacco rules are due later: from 1 January 2027 it will be illegal to sell tobacco to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009. See the site's smoking page for health information.

dizziness-and-vertigo-causes-and-warning.name: Dizziness and vertigo: causes and warning signs
dizziness-and-vertigo-causes-and-warning.headline: Dizziness and vertigo: common causes and the signs that need urgent help
dizziness-and-vertigo-causes-and-warning.summary: Dizziness is common and has many causes, from inner ear problems to low blood pressure. The NHS advises calling 999 when it comes with signs of a stroke.
keyPoints: Vertigo is the feeling that you or the room is spinning, and the NHS says inner ear problems are its most common causes.
The NHS says to call 999 for vertigo with double vision, trouble speaking or weakness or numbness in an arm or leg.
A severe headache or feeling very sick with vertigo calls for an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.
Dizziness that keeps coming back, or comes with hearing, eyesight or pulse changes or fainting, is a reason to contact a GP.

body.heading: Is dizziness the same as vertigo?
body.body: Dizziness is a broad word that people use for several sensations, including light-headedness and a feeling of spinning. Vertigo is a particular kind of dizziness in which it feels as if you or the room is spinning, even when nothing is moving. The NHS says inner ear problems, which affect balance, are the most common causes of vertigo.

body.heading: What causes light-headedness?
body.body: NHS inform lists labyrinthitis, migraine, stress or anxiety, low blood sugar, dehydration and certain prescription medicines among the causes of dizziness. A sudden drop in blood pressure on standing up is another listed cause. Less often, an irregular heart rhythm called atrial fibrillation, or carbon monoxide poisoning, is on the list.

body.heading: What are the common causes of vertigo?
body.body: The NHS vertigo page lists benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis, Ménière’s disease and migraine, and notes that some medicines can also cause it. In BPPV, certain head movements trigger spells of spinning that usually last from a few seconds to a few minutes. Rolling over in bed or tilting the head back to look up are typical triggers. Labyrinthitis is usually caused by a viral infection such as a cold or flu, so antibiotics will not help, and the vertigo usually lasts a few days. Hearing loss and ringing in the ears (tinnitus) can come with labyrinthitis. Ménière’s disease is a rarer cause, with attacks that can include tinnitus, a feeling of fullness in the ear and changing hearing; the NHS says there is no cure but symptoms can be managed.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body: NHS inform advises contacting a GP if dizziness will not go away or keeps coming back. Changes in hearing, eyesight or pulse, or fainting, are further reasons to make contact. For vertigo, the NHS suggests seeing a GP if it comes on suddenly, does not go away, keeps returning or affects daily life.

body.heading: When is it urgent?
body.body: The NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 if vertigo comes with a severe headache, being sick or feeling very sick, or a very high temperature. It says to call 999 or go to A&E if vertigo comes with double vision or loss of vision, hearing loss, trouble speaking, or weakness, numbness or tingling in an arm or a leg. The NHS also advises not to drive yourself to A&E. Dizziness is among the symptoms the NHS lists for stroke, and any sign of stroke is treated as an emergency: the NHS FAST test stands for face, arms, speech and time to call 999.

eatwell-guide-healthy-eating.name: The Eatwell Guide: a balanced diet explained
eatwell-guide-healthy-eating.summary: The Eatwell Guide shows the proportions of food groups in a balanced UK diet, with fruit, vegetables and starchy foods making up just over a third each.
keyPoints: The NHS Eatwell Guide divides food into groups and shows how much of each makes up a balanced diet.
Fruit and vegetables and starchy foods each make up just over a third of the guide, with higher-fibre starchy choices preferred.
NHS advice is at least five portions of a variety of fruit and vegetables a day, and at least two portions of fish a week, one of them oily.
Foods high in fat, salt and sugar sit outside the main groups and are meant to be eaten less often and in small amounts.

body.heading: What is the Eatwell Guide?
body.body: The Eatwell Guide is the UK government's picture of a balanced diet, and the NHS explains it on its Live Well pages. It divides the foods people eat into groups and shows roughly what share of the diet each should make up. Foods and drinks high in fat, salt and sugar sit outside the main groups, and the guide says they should be eaten less often and in small amounts.

body.heading: How much fruit, vegetables and starchy food?
body.body: Fruit and vegetables make up just over a third of the food in the guide. The NHS advises at least five portions of a variety of fruit and vegetables a day. A portion of fresh, canned or frozen fruit or vegetables is 80 grams. Starchy foods also make up just over a third of the guide, and the NHS recommends choosing wholegrain or higher-fibre versions where possible.

body.heading: What about protein, dairy and oils?
body.body: The guide includes beans, pulses, fish, eggs and meat as protein sources, with fish given particular mention. The NHS advises at least two portions of fish a week, including at least one portion of oily fish. For dairy and alternatives the guide points to lower-fat and lower-sugar choices where possible. Unsaturated oils and spreads are the choice for oils, eaten in small amounts.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about fat, sugar and salt?
body.body: NHS healthy eating advice names saturated fat, free sugars and salt as the main things to keep in check. Fruit juice and smoothies are limited to a total of 150 millilitres a day, because they are high in sugar. The NHS says sugary drinks can be swapped for diet, sugar-free or no-added-sugar versions.

body.heading: Where do drinks, breakfast and weight fit in?
body.body: The NHS tips say that balancing the energy taken in from food and drink with the energy used through activity is the key to a healthy weight. They describe a breakfast high in fibre and low in fat, sugar and salt as one way to be part of a balanced diet.

body.heading: How do salt and saturated fat fit in?
body.body: The NHS advises adults and children aged 11 and over to have no more than 6 grams of salt a day, and younger children less. It says about three quarters of the salt people eat comes from packaged foods, which is why labels matter. Salt is linked to high blood pressure, which can lead to heart disease or stroke. Too much saturated fat can increase cholesterol in the blood and so the risk of heart disease, and the NHS suggests swapping towards unsaturated fats such as vegetable oils, oily fish and avocados.

body.heading: What do food labels show?
body.body: UK nutrition labels show energy, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt. Front-of-pack labels use red, amber and green colours to show whether a food is high, medium or low in fat, saturated fat, sugars and salt. The NHS lists sugary drinks, sugary cereals, cakes, biscuits, sweets and alcoholic drinks among the main sources of added sugar, and advises checking labels for sugar content.

fever-in-adults-causes-and-when-to-get-h.headline: High temperature in adults: what usually causes it and when to get help
fever-in-adults-causes-and-when-to-get-h.summary: A high temperature in adults is usually a sign of infection and often settles at home. The NHS advises urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP if it does not improve, and 999 for some warning signs.
keyPoints: The NHS says a high temperature is usually a symptom of an infection.
Home care in the NHS advice includes resting, drinking fluids and, if needed, taking paracetamol or ibuprofen.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if a high temperature is not improving after home treatment or is getting worse.
A rash that does not fade under a glass, a stiff neck, a very painful headache or confusion with a fever are signs the NHS gives for calling 999.

body.heading: What causes a high temperature?
body.body: The NHS says a high temperature is usually a symptom of an infection. Examples of infections that can cause fever include flu, tonsillitis and glandular fever, which have their own NHS pages. Heat exhaustion and heatstroke can also raise body temperature, and the NHS covers them on a separate page.

body.heading: What helps at home?
body.body: NHS advice for a high temperature is to rest and drink plenty of fluids. The NHS also says paracetamol or ibuprofen can be taken to help feel more comfortable, following the instructions on the packet or leaflet. NHS inform also suggests wearing loose, comfortable clothing and avoiding alcohol. Staying away from other people while you have a temperature is also advised, to avoid passing on an infection. A fever caused by a viral infection usually gets better in two to three days.

body.heading: When is it worth speaking to a GP or NHS 111?
body.body: The NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 if a high temperature is not improving after treating it at home, or is getting worse. A high temperature that lasts for five days or more, or that does not come down with paracetamol, is also listed as a reason to seek advice. Severe thirst, or passing less urine than usual, and fever after recent foreign travel are further reasons to ask for advice. NHS 111 is free and open every day of the year, day and night. People with a weakened immune system, people who are pregnant and people aged 60 or over are at higher risk of complications, so help may be needed sooner.

body.heading: Which signs mean 999 or A&E?
body.body: The NHS meningitis page lists a rash that does not fade when pressed, a very painful headache, confusion, and a stiff neck with sensitivity to bright lights among the signs that need immediate action. For a rash, the NHS describes the glass test: pressing a clear glass firmly against the skin to see whether the spots fade. Spots that stay visible through the glass are called a non-blanching rash, and rashes can be harder to see on darker skin, so the palms, soles and tummy are worth checking. NHS-linked guidance also says a fever with chest pain or difficulty breathing needs emergency care, and 999 should be called straight away in a life-threatening situation.

flu-or-cold-how-they-differ.name: Flu or a cold: how they differ
flu-or-cold-how-they-differ.headline: Flu or a cold: how to tell them apart, how long each lasts and when to get help
flu-or-cold-how-they-differ.summary: Flu tends to start faster and feel worse than a cold, with fever, aches and exhaustion; a cold mostly stays in the nose and throat.
keyPoints: Cold and flu symptoms overlap, but flu tends to be more severe and often comes on within hours.
A cold mainly affects the nose and throat and builds up over a couple of days.
Neither illness has a cure, and antibiotics do not work against either.
Sudden chest pain, severe breathlessness or coughing up blood needs 999 or A&E.
NHS 111 or a GP can advise if symptoms get worse or last longer than expected.

body.heading: How do flu and a cold differ?
body.body:
Colds and flu are both infections of the airways, and the NHS describes their symptoms as similar. The main difference is how severe they feel.

Flu tends to be more severe than a cold. A cold mostly affects the nose and throat, while flu can also bring a fever, aches and exhaustion.

That difference in reach is the most useful clue. A person with a cold usually feels unwell in the nose and throat but is often able to carry on with some normal activity, whereas flu more often leaves a person feeling run down all over.

body.heading: How quickly do the symptoms start?
body.body:
Speed of onset is another difference the NHS pages point to. Flu tends to come on suddenly, often within hours.

A cold usually builds more gradually, over about two to three days. People often notice a sore throat or a blocked or runny nose first, and other symptoms follow.

body.heading: How long do they last?
body.body:
Most people start to feel better from a cold within about one to two weeks. Flu usually improves within about a week.

Tiredness can linger for longer after flu, even when the other symptoms have settled. Timings vary between people, and the NHS pages for each illness give the usual picture rather than a fixed rule.

body.heading: What treatment is there?
body.body:
There is no cure for a cold or for flu. The NHS says the usual approach is to rest and drink fluids while the body clears the infection.

Pharmacy medicines can ease symptoms, and a pharmacist can talk through the options. Antibiotics do not help, because both illnesses are caused by viruses rather than bacteria.

A flu vaccine protects against flu, but it does not protect against colds.

body.heading: When should someone get medical help?
body.body:
The NHS separates emergencies from problems that can wait for a call or an appointment.

Sudden chest pain, severe difficulty breathing or coughing up blood is an emergency, and the route is 999 or A&E.

For less urgent worries, NHS 111 or the GP can advise. The NHS gives these as reasons to get in touch: symptoms that get worse, a high temperature that lasts for more than three days, symptoms that carry on beyond about ten days, or a cough that continues for more than three weeks.

People with long-term conditions such as diabetes, asthma or heart disease are advised to seek advice sooner, because flu and colds can hit them harder.

body.heading: Is it flu, a cold or something else?
body.body:
Other infections can look like flu or a cold. The UKHSA publishes a guide to the signs and symptoms of flu, COVID-19 and colds, and the NHS pages for each illness set out what to look for.

When symptoms are unusual, severe or not settling as expected, the safest step is to ask NHS 111 or the GP rather than to guess from a list of symptoms.

healthy-weight-bmi-explained.name: Healthy weight: what BMI shows and what it misses
healthy-weight-bmi-explained.summary: BMI is an NHS check on whether weight suits height, but it cannot tell muscle from fat, so waist size and a GP discussion add to it.
keyPoints: The NHS BMI calculator checks whether a person is a healthy weight for their height.
BMI cannot tell muscle from fat, so very muscular people may be rated overweight and people who lose muscle with age may still fall in the healthy range.
The NHS says Black, Asian and some other minority ethnic groups have a higher risk of some long-term conditions at a lower BMI.
NHS treatment for obesity ranges from lifestyle changes and weight management programmes to medicines and surgery.

body.heading: What does BMI measure?
body.body: Body mass index, or BMI, is calculated from height and weight, and the NHS calculator uses it to check whether an adult is a healthy weight for their height. The calculator shows which category a result falls in, and the NHS gives a different healthy range for Black, Asian and some other minority ethnic groups. The reason given is that these groups have a higher risk of developing some long-term conditions, such as type 2 diabetes, at a lower BMI.

body.heading: What are the limits of BMI?
body.body: BMI cannot tell the difference between muscle and fat, so it measures whether someone is carrying too much weight rather than too much fat. Very muscular people and athletes may be rated overweight or obese despite low body fat. Adults who lose muscle as they get older may fall in the healthy weight range even though they may be carrying excess fat.

body.heading: Why does waist size matter?
body.body: The NHS gives a method for measuring the waist: find the bottom of the ribs and the top of the hips, place a tape measure midway between them, and measure after breathing out naturally. The NHS says a waist measurement that is large compared with height may mean increased health risks such as heart disease, type 2 diabetes and stroke. The NHS says a BMI result can be a starting point for a discussion with a GP about weight and general health. A GP may also check blood pressure, blood glucose and cholesterol levels, and waist circumference.

body.heading: What treatment does the NHS offer?
body.body: The NHS says it can be hard to lose weight, and that some people need extra support or treatment to lose weight and keep it off. Options include lifestyle changes, weight management programmes, medicines and surgery. NHS England describes specialist weight management services as multidisciplinary, with doctors, dietitians, specialist nurses and psychologists. Some medicines used for weight loss, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, can only be prescribed through a specialist weight management service.

body.heading: What health risks are linked to excess weight?
body.body: Obesity is linked to type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, musculoskeletal disorders, infertility and psychiatric disorders, according to clinical sources.

body.heading: Why does weight change?
body.body: The NHS describes overweight and obesity as having more body fat than the body needs. It can happen when a person eats or drinks more than the body needs or does not do enough physical activity. Other factors listed include genes, some medicines such as certain steroids, antidepressants and beta blockers, and conditions such as an underactive thyroid.

body.heading: What does a GP check, and what support is free?
body.body: A GP can arrange checks such as a blood test for type 2 diabetes and tests for cholesterol and blood pressure. The NHS offers a free 12-week weight loss plan as an app and a downloadable guide. The NHS says that for someone living with obesity, losing about 3 per cent of starting body weight can reduce the risk of obesity-related complications.

heart-attack-cardiac-arrest-and-angina.name: Heart attack, cardiac arrest and angina
heart-attack-cardiac-arrest-and-angina.headline: Heart attack, cardiac arrest and angina: the differences and when to call 999
heart-attack-cardiac-arrest-and-angina.summary: A heart attack is a blocked blood supply to the heart muscle, cardiac arrest is the heart stopping, and angina is chest pain that eases with rest.
keyPoints: A heart attack happens when a coronary artery becomes blocked and the heart muscle loses its blood supply.
In a cardiac arrest the heart stops pumping effectively, the person collapses and is not breathing normally.
Angina is chest pain from reduced blood flow to the heart and is a sign of coronary heart disease.
Angina symptoms usually ease with rest or a nitrate medicine, whereas heart attack symptoms usually do not.
For a suspected heart attack or cardiac arrest the NHS says to call 999 straight away.

body.heading: What is the difference between a heart attack and cardiac arrest?
body.body:
The two terms are often mixed up, but the NHS and the British Heart Foundation (BHF) treat them as different emergencies.

A heart attack happens when one of the coronary arteries becomes blocked. The heart muscle is cut off from its blood supply and can be damaged if the blockage is not treated. The person is usually conscious and breathing.

In a cardiac arrest the heart stops pumping effectively. The person collapses, does not respond and is not breathing normally. The BHF says a heart attack can sometimes lead to a cardiac arrest.

body.heading: What is angina?
body.body:
Angina is chest pain or discomfort that happens when the heart muscle does not get enough blood because the coronary arteries are partly narrowed. It is a sign of coronary heart disease rather than a heart attack in itself.

The NHS says angina can feel like a mild, uncomfortable sensation, sometimes similar to indigestion. It is often brought on by physical activity or stress and usually passes with rest or a nitrate medicine.

Angina is not usually life-threatening, but the BHF notes that it can be a sign of a higher risk of a heart attack.

body.heading: What are the symptoms of a heart attack?
body.body:
The NHS lists chest pain that feels like pressure, heaviness, tightness or squeezing. The pain can spread to the arms, jaw, neck, back or tummy.

Other signs include feeling sick, sweating, shortness of breath and light-headedness. Some people have few symptoms, and the NHS says this is more common in older people and people with diabetes.

A key difference from angina is that heart attack symptoms are not usually relieved by a nitrate tablet or spray.

body.heading: What are the signs of a cardiac arrest?
body.body:
A person in cardiac arrest loses consciousness. They do not respond to touch or speech, and they are not breathing normally.

Without treatment a cardiac arrest is usually fatal within minutes, according to the BHF, which is why speed matters.

body.heading: When should someone call 999?
body.body:
The NHS says to call 999 immediately if someone may be having a heart attack, even if the symptoms seem mild.

If someone seems to be in cardiac arrest, the NHS advises calling 999 and starting CPR, with the call handler giving instructions.

For angina, a GP appointment is the usual route for a first episode of chest pain. The BHF says that chest pain that comes on suddenly and does not stop after a few minutes of rest could be a heart attack, and that is a 999 situation.

body.heading: How are they diagnosed and treated?
body.body:
A heart attack is usually assessed with an ECG, which records the heart's electrical activity, and a blood test for troponin, a protein released when the heart muscle is damaged. The site's pages on these tests give more detail.

Treatment aims to restore blood flow to the heart muscle as quickly as possible. Angina is managed with medicines and changes that reduce the strain on the heart, and the care team decides the plan.

heartburn-acid-reflux-and-gord.name: Heartburn, acid reflux and GORD
heartburn-acid-reflux-and-gord.headline: Heartburn, acid reflux and GORD: what they are and when to see a GP
heartburn-acid-reflux-and-gord.summary: Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest from acid reflux; when it keeps happening it is called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD).
keyPoints: Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest caused by stomach acid travelling up towards the throat.
When reflux keeps happening it is called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD.
Lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines are the usual first steps, and a pharmacist can advise on options.
Difficulty swallowing, unintentional weight loss, repeated vomiting or blood in vomit or stools need prompt medical advice.
A GP can prescribe acid-reducing medicine and arrange tests if symptoms continue.

body.heading: What is heartburn, and how does it relate to GORD?
body.body:
Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest. NHS sources describe it as caused by stomach acid travelling up towards the throat, which is known as acid reflux.

If it keeps happening, the condition is called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD. The terms heartburn, acid reflux and GORD overlap, and the difference lies mostly in how often and how long the symptoms occur.

body.heading: What are the symptoms?
body.body:
The main symptoms of acid reflux are heartburn and an unpleasant sour taste in the mouth caused by stomach acid. Some people also have a cough, a hoarse voice, bloating or feeling sick.

Symptoms tend to get worse after eating, when lying down or when bending over.

body.heading: What can bring it on?
body.body:
NHS sources list a number of contributors: being overweight, smoking, drinking alcohol, eating large meals or eating close to bedtime, stress, having a hiatus hernia, and pregnancy.

Some medicines, including anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen, can also play a part. A pharmacist or GP can review whether any medicine a person takes is relevant, and the person should not change a prescribed medicine without that advice.

body.heading: What helps?
body.body:
Lifestyle changes are usually the first step. NHS advice includes avoiding late meals, raising the head of the bed, cutting down on trigger foods such as coffee, chocolate and fatty or spicy food, and losing weight where that is relevant. Stopping smoking and cutting down on alcohol are also advised.

Antacids and alginates, which are available from pharmacies, can ease symptoms, and a pharmacist can talk through the options.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body:
A GP appointment is the usual route if lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines do not help, or if heartburn happens most days.

Some symptoms need prompt attention, by contacting the GP or NHS 111. NHS sources list difficulty swallowing, unintentional weight loss, repeated vomiting, severe or worsening pain, being 55 or older with new symptoms, and blood in vomit or in stools.

Chest pain can also be a sign of a heart problem. Sudden chest pain, pain spreading to the arm, neck or jaw, or breathlessness is a reason to call 999.

body.heading: What can a GP offer?
body.body:
A GP may prescribe a proton pump inhibitor, a medicine that reduces the amount of acid the stomach makes. NHS 111 Wales says people usually need this type of medicine for a limited course, depending on how severe the reflux is, and that anyone whose symptoms return afterwards should go back to the GP, as longer-term treatment may be needed.

If symptoms continue despite treatment, or if there are warning signs, a GP may arrange a gastroscopy, a test that uses a thin camera to look at the upper gut.

heavy-periods-causes-tests-and-treatment.name: Heavy periods: causes, tests and treatment
heavy-periods-causes-tests-and-treatment.headline: Heavy periods: what can cause them, which checks a GP offers and how they are treated
heavy-periods-causes-tests-and-treatment.summary: Heavy periods are common and often have no clear cause, but fibroids, endometriosis and other conditions can be behind them. The NHS advises a GP visit when they affect daily life.
keyPoints: Some people naturally have heavier periods than others, and the NHS says help is available when they affect daily life.
Often there is no underlying medical reason, though fibroids, endometriosis and some other conditions can cause heavy periods.
The NHS advises seeing a GP if heavy periods affect life, have lasted some time, come with severe pain, or if there is bleeding between periods or after sex.
Treatment choices include some contraceptives, medicines to reduce bleeding and surgery, and heavy periods do not always need treatment.

body.heading: What counts as a heavy period?
body.body: The NHS describes heavy periods in practical terms, such as needing to change pads or tampons every one to two hours. Some people naturally have heavier periods than others, but the NHS says that when periods are so heavy that they affect life, help is available. Feeling tired or short of breath, or avoiding daily activities because of periods, are other signs that bleeding may be a problem.

body.heading: What causes them?
body.body: Heavy periods often have no underlying cause. Fibroids, which are non-cancerous growths in or around the womb, are a common identifiable cause. Other conditions that can cause heavy periods include endometriosis, adenomyosis, polycystic ovary syndrome and pelvic inflammatory disease. Some medicines, such as anticoagulants and some chemotherapy medicines, can also be responsible. Rarely, heavy periods can be a sign of womb cancer.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body: NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP if heavy periods affect your life, have lasted for some time, or come with severe pain. Bleeding between periods or after sex is also a reason to see a GP. For severe period or pelvic pain that is worse than usual and not helped by painkillers, the NHS advises getting urgent advice, from NHS 111 if needed.

body.heading: Which tests might a GP arrange?
body.body: A GP can investigate why bleeding is heavy, which may include a physical examination, blood tests or scans. A blood test to look for iron deficiency anaemia is usually offered to people with heavy periods. A pregnancy test, an ultrasound scan and, less often, a hysteroscopy (a look inside the womb with a small camera) may follow. Keeping a record of the bleeding before the appointment is suggested to help the discussion.

body.heading: How are heavy periods treated?
body.body: Heavy periods do not always need to be treated. If they affect daily life, options include a hormone-releasing intrauterine system (IUS) or the combined contraceptive pill. Medicines to reduce the bleeding, such as tranexamic acid, and anti-inflammatory painkillers such as mefenamic acid or naproxen are also used. Surgical options exist, and some treatments affect whether a person can become pregnant, so the clinician discusses this when treatment is chosen. If treatments have not worked, or a condition may be causing the bleeding, a referral to a hospital specialist may follow.

high-blood-pressure-what-happens-next.name: High blood pressure: what happens next
high-blood-pressure-what-happens-next.headline: High blood pressure: how it is found, what causes it and what treatment involves
high-blood-pressure-what-happens-next.summary: High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms and is found by measuring it; treatment starts with lifestyle changes and may include medicine.
keyPoints: High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, and the only way to know is to have it measured.
In most people no single cause is found; age, family history, ethnicity and lifestyle all play a part.
Readings taken at home or by a 24-hour monitor can be used alongside clinic readings to confirm the diagnosis.
Lifestyle changes are the first step, and a GP may prescribe medicine if blood pressure is very high or stays high.
Chest pain that does not go away, or pain spreading to the arm, neck, jaw or back, needs 999.

body.heading: What does a blood pressure reading mean?
body.body:
Blood pressure is the force of blood against the walls of the arteries. A reading gives two numbers: the pressure when the heart beats and the pressure between beats. The site's page on blood pressure measurement explains how they are taken.

The NHS and NICE use different thresholds for clinic and home readings, and a GP uses them to decide whether blood pressure is high. A clinician can say which applies to the person.

body.heading: Does high blood pressure cause symptoms?
body.body:
Usually not. The NHS says high blood pressure often has no symptoms, so many people do not know they have it, and the only way to find out is to have it measured. Rarely it can cause headaches, blurred vision or chest pain.

Over time, the NHS says, untreated high blood pressure raises the chance of problems such as stroke and heart disease.

body.heading: What causes it?
body.body:
For most people there is no obvious cause, which is called essential hypertension, and it can run in families. In a small number of people there is an underlying cause, such as a kidney or adrenal gland condition.

The NHS says risk rises with age, with Black African or Black Caribbean ethnicity, and with a family history. Smoking, drinking too much alcohol, being overweight and not being active are also linked.

body.heading: How is the diagnosis confirmed?
body.body:
A single clinic reading is usually followed by other checks. NICE advises confirming raised clinic readings with home monitoring or with a 24-hour ambulatory monitor, which takes readings through the day.

Some people have higher readings in a clinic than at home, sometimes called the white coat effect, which is one reason these extra checks are used. A GP may also arrange blood and urine tests and an ECG to look for effects on the body and for other causes.

body.heading: What does treatment involve?
body.body:
Lifestyle changes come first for many people. The NHS lists a balanced diet, regular physical activity, cutting down on salt and alcohol, losing weight where relevant, and not smoking.

A GP will usually prescribe medicine if blood pressure is very high, if the person has a higher risk of heart attack or stroke, or if it stays high after lifestyle changes. Several types are used, including ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers and diuretics, and some people need more than one.

The NHS advises against stopping blood pressure medicine without speaking to the GP first.

body.heading: When is it an emergency?
body.body:
The NHS says to call 999 for chest pain that does not go away, or pain spreading to the arm, neck, jaw or back.

A very high reading with symptoms such as severe headache, vision changes or confusion should be discussed urgently with NHS 111 or a GP, and 999 is the route if the person is very unwell.

how-long-antidepressants-take-to-work.name: How long antidepressants take to work
how-long-antidepressants-take-to-work.headline: How long antidepressants take to work, and what the NHS says about side effects and stopping
how-long-antidepressants-take-to-work.summary: The NHS says antidepressants usually start to help after 1 to 2 weeks and can take up to 8 weeks to work fully.
keyPoints: The NHS says antidepressants usually take 1 to 2 weeks to start having an effect and can take up to 8 weeks to work fully.
For sertraline and citalopram the NHS says it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to work fully, with some people feeling better after 1 to 2 weeks.
Early side effects such as feeling sick, headaches and trouble sleeping are common, and the NHS says they usually ease after a couple of weeks.
The NHS and NICE both say that stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, so changes to the dose are decided with the prescriber.
If a person or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 (free, any time) are other routes.

body.heading: How long do antidepressants take to work?
body.body:
The NHS says antidepressants usually take 1 to 2 weeks to start having an effect. They can take up to 8 weeks to work fully. For sertraline, the NHS says it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to work fully, although some people start to feel better after 1 to 2 weeks. For citalopram, the NHS gives the same pattern, with a usual 4 to 6 weeks before the full benefit and some improvement possible after 1 to 2 weeks.

Both medicines belong to a group called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. For citalopram, the NHS advises against stopping after only 1 or 2 weeks just because it seems not to be helping, since the full benefit takes longer to appear.

body.heading: What can happen in the first weeks?
body.body:
The NHS lists nausea, headaches and diarrhoea among the common side effects of sertraline. It also lists dizziness or drowsiness, dry mouth and sleep problems. For citalopram, common effects include tiredness, feeling nervous, dry mouth and sweating. The NHS says common side effects like these are usually mild and go away after a couple of weeks as the body gets used to the medicine.

The NHS lists sexual problems, such as a lower sex drive, among the common side effects of citalopram. Sertraline can make a person feel more or less hungry than usual, so weight may go down or up at the start, the NHS says. The NHS suggests avoiding alcohol with sertraline because it can stop the medicine working properly. It also says grapefruit juice can increase the amount of sertraline in the body and the risk of side effects.

If side effects last beyond 1 or 2 weeks, the NHS suggests asking a pharmacist or doctor about them.

body.heading: What if nothing seems to change?
body.body: The NHS says a GP may recommend trying a different antidepressant if the first one is not helping. People respond differently to different antidepressants, so a change of medicine can sometimes help. Anyone worried about their progress can raise it with a GP or pharmacist.

body.heading: Why is stopping suddenly a question for the prescriber?
body.body:
The NHS says antidepressants should not be stopped suddenly, because this may cause withdrawal symptoms. For citalopram, the NHS says the doctor will usually recommend reducing the dose gradually over several weeks, or longer after a long course. For sertraline, the NHS says stopping is usually done by reducing the dose gradually.

NICE says reducing the dose in stages, known as tapering, helps to lessen withdrawal effects, and that the taper is agreed with the person's healthcare professional. NICE guidance for adults with depression also says people who want to stop should talk to the person who prescribed the medicine. Tapering is typically needed, and most people manage to stop successfully. The NHS adds that stopping too early can make depression come back.

body.heading: How long does treatment usually last?
body.body: The NHS says a course of antidepressants usually lasts for at least 6 months after a person starts to feel better. For citalopram, the NHS says most doctors recommend taking antidepressants for 6 months to a year. For sertraline, the NHS says most doctors recommend treatment for 6 months to a year after a person no longer feels depressed. The decision to stop or continue depends on symptoms and how well the medicine is working, and is made with the prescriber.

body.heading: Where can someone get help in a crisis?
body.body: If a person or someone else is in immediate danger, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option. Samaritans can be called free on 116 123 at any time of the day or night. In England, adults aged 18 or over can refer themselves directly to NHS talking therapies without a GP referral. These services are for anxiety and depression and are not for urgent crisis help.

ibuprofen-and-paracetamol-together.name: Ibuprofen and paracetamol together: NHS view
ibuprofen-and-paracetamol-together.headline: Can you take ibuprofen and paracetamol together? What the NHS says
ibuprofen-and-paracetamol-together.summary: The NHS says adults can take paracetamol and ibuprofen together if needed, but children should not be given them at the same time.
keyPoints: The NHS says adults can take paracetamol and ibuprofen at the same time if needed, and NHS inform says the two can be taken together if required.
For children, the NHS says paracetamol and ibuprofen should not be given at the same time but one at a time.
The NHS lists groups who should avoid ibuprofen or check first, including people with repeated stomach ulcers or bleeding, asthma, or severe kidney failure.
Many cold and flu products contain paracetamol or ibuprofen, so using several products can make it easy to take more than the recommended amount.
The NHS says to call 999 for signs of a serious allergic reaction, and to get urgent advice from NHS 111 or a doctor for other serious effects such as stomach bleeding or kidney problems.

body.heading: What is each medicine used for?
body.body: Ibuprofen belongs to a group of painkillers called non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or NSAIDs. The NHS describes ibuprofen as a painkiller that also treats inflammation. It describes paracetamol as a painkiller for pain and high temperature. For a dental abscess, NHS inform says ibuprofen is the preferred painkiller, and paracetamol can be taken instead if ibuprofen cannot be taken for medical reasons. The NHS also says that if you need pain relief while taking warfarin, paracetamol is the one to take instead of ibuprofen.

body.heading: Can adults take both at the same time?
body.body: For adults, the NHS says paracetamol can be taken at the same time as ibuprofen if needed. It also says paracetamol can be taken with other painkillers that do not contain paracetamol, such as ibuprofen, aspirin or codeine. NHS inform, the NHS information service for Scotland, also says the two can be taken together if required. For a dental abscess, it says that if one painkiller does not work, taking both paracetamol and ibuprofen may help. The advice is different for children. For them, the NHS says paracetamol can be given alongside ibuprofen but not at the same time, and the two should be given one at a time.

body.heading: Who is told to check with a pharmacist or doctor first?
body.body: The NHS lists several groups who should avoid ibuprofen or check with a professional before using it. These include people who have had an allergic reaction to aspirin or other NSAIDs, with signs such as wheezing, a runny nose or skin reactions. They also include people who have had a hole in the stomach, bleeding in the stomach or a stomach ulcer more than once, and people with severe heart, kidney or liver failure. Asthma, hay fever and allergies are also on the NHS list. The NHS also says to avoid ibuprofen in pregnancy unless a doctor or pharmacist advises it, and to check with a pharmacist or doctor when breastfeeding. People over 65 are more likely to get stomach ulcers with ibuprofen, according to the NHS. Other medicines can interact with ibuprofen. The NHS interactions page lists warfarin and other anticoagulants, medicines for high blood pressure, steroids such as prednisolone, certain antibiotics and some antidepressants. It advises against taking ginkgo biloba with ibuprofen because it can increase the chance of bleeding. For other herbal products, it says there is not enough information to say whether they can be taken with ibuprofen. NHS inform advises anyone already taking other medication to check with a pharmacist first.

body.heading: Why do other products containing the same ingredients matter?
body.body: Many cold and flu products contain paracetamol or ibuprofen. NHS inform says this makes it easy to take more than the recommended dose. The NHS says to avoid taking other medicines that contain paracetamol at the same time as paracetamol, such as cold and flu remedies, because too much can be dangerous. It adds that taking two different medicines that contain paracetamol carries a risk of overdose, and that too much paracetamol can sometimes damage the liver. For ibuprofen, the NHS says to check the label of cold and cough remedies for aspirin, ibuprofen or other NSAIDs. Taking ibuprofen with other NSAIDs such as aspirin or naproxen is not advised without speaking to a pharmacist or doctor, because side effects such as stomach ache become more likely.

body.heading: What side effects do the NHS pages describe?
body.body: The NHS lists common side effects of ibuprofen as indigestion, stomach aches, feeling sick, being sick and headaches. Serious ones include stomach ulcers or bleeding in the stomach, and allergic reactions. The NHS also lists kidney problems, such as swollen ankles or blood in the urine, as a reason to get urgent advice. For paracetamol, the NHS says there may be no obvious symptoms at first after taking too much, so feeling well does not rule out harm.

body.heading: When should someone get help, and from whom?
body.body: For signs of a serious allergic reaction to ibuprofen, such as swollen lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or difficult breathing or a tight throat, the NHS says to call 999. The NHS also says to call 999 for severe chest or stomach pain, which can signal a hole in the stomach or gut, and for difficulty breathing or worsening asthma symptoms. Vomiting blood or black, tar-like poo can be signs of bleeding in the stomach, and the NHS says to get urgent advice from NHS 111 or a doctor. Swollen ankles or blood in the urine can point to a kidney problem, and the NHS says to contact NHS 111 or a doctor. If too much paracetamol has been taken, the NHS says to contact NHS 111 for advice, even when the person feels well. For questions that are not urgent, NHS inform says to speak to a pharmacist if unsure.

kidney-stones-symptoms-and-treatment.name: Kidney stones: symptoms and treatment
kidney-stones-symptoms-and-treatment.headline: Kidney stones: symptoms, how they are diagnosed and how they are treated
kidney-stones-symptoms-and-treatment.summary: Kidney stones are hard deposits that can cause severe pain in the side or back; many pass on their own, while large ones may need a procedure.
keyPoints: Kidney stones form when chemicals from urine build up in the kidneys, and small stones may cause no symptoms.
Larger stones can cause severe pain in the side or lower back that comes and goes, sometimes with nausea or blood in the urine.
A GP can often diagnose kidney stones from symptoms and history, with urine and blood tests and sometimes a scan.
Most stones can be treated at home with medicines and plenty of fluids; larger stones may need to be broken up or removed.
Severe pain, a high temperature or feeling hot, cold or shivery needs urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP.

body.heading: What are kidney stones?
body.body:
Kidney stones are hard lumps that form in the kidneys. The NHS says they are caused by chemicals from urine building up in the kidneys. They can sit in the kidney or travel down the tubes that lead to the bladder.

Small stones may cause no symptoms and are sometimes found by chance on an X-ray or scan done for another reason.

body.heading: What symptoms can they cause?
body.body:
Larger stones can cause pain in the side of the tummy or the lower back, and the pain may spread towards the groin. It can come and go in waves.

Other symptoms can include nausea or vomiting, needing to pass urine more often, cloudy urine, blood in the urine, and a high temperature.

body.heading: What causes them?
body.body:
The NHS says kidney stones can be caused by dehydration, by some medicines, and by some medical conditions. Not drinking enough water raises the chance of getting one.

A GP or pharmacist can say whether a medicine the person takes may be relevant. Prescribed medicines should not be stopped without that advice.

body.heading: How are kidney stones diagnosed?
body.body:
A GP can usually diagnose kidney stones from the symptoms and medical history. Urine and blood tests may be used.

If the pain is severe, the NHS says the person should be referred to hospital for an urgent scan. A CT scan is usually offered to adults, and an ultrasound scan to pregnant women and to children under 16.

body.heading: How are they treated?
body.body:
Most kidney stones can be treated at home. The NHS says this usually means painkillers, anti-sickness medicine, medicines that help a stone pass, and drinking plenty of water.

Larger stones may need to be broken up or removed. One option is shock wave lithotripsy, which uses sound waves from outside the body to break the stone into smaller pieces that can pass in the urine. Other procedures use a thin scope to reach the stone.

body.heading: When should someone get urgent help?
body.body:
The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or contacting NHS 111 for anyone with kidney stone symptoms who is in severe pain, or has a high temperature, or feels hot, cold or shivery.

A fever with a stone can mean the kidney is infected, which needs prompt treatment. Being unable to pass urine is also a reason to seek urgent help, and 999 is the route if the person is very unwell.
