metformin-what-to-expect.name: Metformin: what to expect when starting
metformin-what-to-expect.headline: Metformin: what the NHS says to expect when starting it
metformin-what-to-expect.summary: The NHS describes metformin as usually the first medicine for type 2 diabetes. Side effects are mostly stomach-related and mostly ease.
keyPoints: The NHS says metformin is usually the first medicine prescribed for type 2 diabetes.
Common side effects are stomach-related; the NHS says most ease after a couple of weeks, and taking tablets with a meal or slow-release tablets can help.
The NHS says long-term use can cause vitamin B12 deficiency, so a doctor may check B12 levels.
The NHS says illness with vomiting, diarrhoea or fever risks dehydration, and metformin may need pausing before surgery or scans using dye.
For side effects, a GP or diabetes team can advise; the NHS says call NHS 111 for other serious side effects and 999 for suspected lactic acidosis or anaphylaxis.

body.heading: What is metformin used for?
body.body: The NHS describes metformin as a medicine used to treat type 2 diabetes, and says it is usually the first choice prescribed for it. It can also be prescribed to help improve ovulation in polycystic ovary syndrome, which the NHS pages call PMOS. The NHS says it reduces the amount of sugar the liver releases into the blood and helps the body respond better to insulin. The NHS also says it does not usually cause weight gain.

body.heading: How is metformin taken?
body.body: The NHS says metformin comes as two kinds of tablet: standard tablets and slow-release tablets. Standard tablets act quickly and may be taken several times a day, while slow-release ones work gradually, so they are taken less often. The NHS says the prescriber sets the amount, and that when standard tablets are first started the amount is usually increased slowly, which reduces the chance of side effects. It says it is best to take metformin with, or just after, a meal, and that tablets are swallowed whole with water rather than chewed. For diabetes, the NHS says treatment is usually for life, and that stopping suddenly makes blood sugar levels go up. The prescriber's instructions and the leaflet in the pack remain the guide for any one person.

body.heading: What side effects are common, and do they settle?
body.body: The NHS lists feeling sick, being sick, diarrhoea, tummy pain, loss of appetite and a change in taste among the common side effects. It says most of these should ease after a couple of weeks as the body gets used to the medicine, although some can last longer. The NHS says taking the tablets with a meal and increasing the amount slowly can reduce them. If side effects are too troublesome, it says a doctor may suggest slow-release tablets. Diabetes UK also says early stomach-related effects usually settle within a few weeks. For people on standard-release tablets who have these effects, Diabetes UK advises speaking to a GP or diabetes team, who can say whether slow-release tablets might suit them.

body.heading: What about vitamin B12?
body.body: The NHS says that taking metformin for a long time can lead to vitamin B12 deficiency, which can leave a person feeling very tired. Diabetes UK likewise says prolonged use, especially at higher doses, can lower vitamin B12 levels, which matter for red blood cells and nerves. The NHS says a doctor can check B12 levels in the blood, and that vitamin B12 supplements help if levels get too low. Diabetes UK says anyone with symptoms of deficiency should ask their diabetes team or GP about a blood test.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about illness, dehydration, alcohol and scans?
body.body: The NHS says that being ill with vomiting, diarrhoea or a high temperature while taking metformin carries a risk of dehydration. On alcohol, the NHS advises limiting how much is drunk while taking metformin, because alcohol can increase the risk of serious side effects, and says drinking more than its suggested limit can raise the risk of low blood sugar. The NHS also says a doctor may tell a person to stop metformin a few days before an operation or medical tests, and that it may need pausing before scans that use iodine-based dye. Anyone unsure what to do when unwell or before a procedure can ask a GP or pharmacist.

body.heading: Who may not be able to take metformin?
body.body: The NHS says most adults and children aged 10 and over can take metformin, but it is not suitable for everyone. Situations to raise with a doctor before starting include a past allergic reaction to metformin or another medicine, uncontrolled diabetes, liver or kidney problems, a severe infection, heart failure treatment or a recent heart attack, and heavy alcohol use. The NHS says metformin can be taken in pregnancy, alone or with insulin, after checking with a doctor, and that it can usually be taken while breastfeeding because only tiny amounts pass into breast milk. It also says there is no evidence that metformin lowers fertility in men or women.

body.heading: What if a dose is missed, or serious symptoms appear?
body.body: The NHS says not to take two doses to make up for a forgotten one. For side effects that are troublesome, the NHS says a doctor may suggest slow-release tablets, and Diabetes UK points people to a GP or diabetes team. The NHS describes serious side effects as uncommon and lists lactic acidosis (too much acid in the blood), anaphylaxis (a severe allergic reaction) and liver inflammation (hepatitis). It says to call 999 if lactic acidosis or anaphylaxis is suspected, and to call NHS 111 for any other serious side effect. NHS 111 is also the NHS route if more than the prescribed amount has been taken.

mhra-approves-lurbinectedin-small-cell-l.summary: The MHRA approved lurbinectedin (Zepzelca) on 23 September 2026 for adults with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, as maintenance treatment with atezolizumab.
keyPoints: The MHRA approved lurbinectedin (Zepzelca) on 23 September 2026 for adults with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer.
It is approved in combination with atezolizumab as maintenance treatment.
The MHRA says it will keep the safety and effectiveness of lurbinectedin under close review.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
The MHRA says it has approved lurbinectedin (Zepzelca) for adults with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer. It is approved in combination with atezolizumab as maintenance treatment, for adults whose cancer has not progressed after first-line induction treatment with atezolizumab, carboplatin and etoposide.

The MHRA describes a main study of 483 adults with extensive-stage disease.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
The MHRA explains that lurbinectedin attaches to DNA inside cancer cells, which damages it and blocks cell growth, leading to cell death. The MHRA says it will keep the safety and effectiveness of the medicine under close review.

Approval by the MHRA is a licensing decision. It is separate from decisions on NHS funding. The site's lung cancer page explains the condition.

mhra-new-safeguards-antidepressant-safet.name: MHRA adds antidepressant safety safeguards
mhra-new-safeguards-antidepressant-safet.summary: On 15 October 2026 the MHRA announced new safeguards for antidepressant safety information after a review of 28 antidepressants, covering suicidal thoughts and behaviours and sexual dysfunction that continues after stopping.
keyPoints: The MHRA announced the measures on 15 October 2026 after a review by an expert working group of the Commission on Human Medicines.
The review looked at how two risks are communicated to patients for 28 antidepressant medicines.
The measures include a boxed warning in patient leaflets, a patient card and a new safety leaflet.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
The MHRA says an expert working group of the Commission on Human Medicines has finished a detailed review of how the potential risks of 28 antidepressant medicines are communicated to patients. The review began after concerns from patients and families about the information in patient information leaflets.

The two risks are suicidal thoughts and behaviours, and sexual dysfunction that continues after treatment is stopped.

body.heading: What changes
body.body:
The MHRA lists a new boxed warning in the leaflets, to highlight information on suicidal thoughts and behaviours and point to where help can be found. A new patient card, in digital or paper form, reinforces key safety messages. A new safety leaflet is being developed with other health system partners and can be given out by healthcare professionals. The MHRA has also published a public assessment report on the review.

If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999. For urgent mental health help, NHS 111 offers a mental health option, and Samaritans are free to call on 116 123 at any time. The site's SSRI, sertraline and citalopram pages cover this group of medicines.

The recall covers all strengths of Xeal Pharma's clopidogrel oral suspension and oral solution, which contain less than the labelled amount.
The notice says no reports of patient harm have been received.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
The MHRA notice covers all strengths of Xeal Pharma's Clopidogrel Oral Suspension and Clopidogrel Oral Solution, which contain less than the labelled amount of clopidogrel. The notice attributes this to a formulation error. Affected batches contain 76% of the required amount, and the recall covers all batches produced before the notice.

Pharmacists and wholesalers are told to stop supplying the affected batches and to quarantine remaining stock.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
Based on Xeal Pharma's risk assessment, the notice says patient harm is not anticipated in patients receiving the product for long-term preventative treatment, and that no reports of patient harm have been received. The notice says these are unlicensed products and that no licensed clopidogrel oral suspension or solution is available.

Xeal Pharma has confirmed that future stock will be made with the correct strength. Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet medicine, and the site has a page on it.

migraine-and-tension-headache-compared.name: Migraine and tension headache compared
migraine-and-tension-headache-compared.headline: Migraine and tension-type headache compared: features, treatment and warning signs
migraine-and-tension-headache-compared.summary: Tension headache is usually a dull, tight pressure on both sides of the head, while migraine often throbs and brings nausea or sensitivity to light.
keyPoints: Tension-type headache usually causes a pressing or tightening pain on both sides of the head, with mild to moderate severity.
Migraine is often a throbbing pain that can be moderate to severe, with nausea, vomiting and sensitivity to light and sound.
Some people have an aura before a migraine, and attacks last longer than a typical tension headache.
Painkillers help both, but frequent use of painkillers can itself cause headaches.
A sudden, extremely painful headache, or a headache with confusion, vision loss or a stiff neck and high temperature, needs 999 or A&E.

body.heading: What does a tension headache feel like?
body.body:
Tension-type headache typically causes a pressing or tightening pain on both sides of the head, and the area can feel tender to the touch. NICE describes the pain as mild to moderate and not made worse by routine activity.

The NHS says a tension headache is commonly felt for 30 minutes to several hours, but it can last for days. MedlinePlus says it usually does not come with nausea, vomiting, or sensitivity to light and sound.

body.heading: What does a migraine feel like?
body.body:
NICE describes migraine as a headache that is usually throbbing or pulsating, often moderate to severe, and that can be on one side or both. Nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light and sound are common.

Attacks typically last for hours, and some people have an aura, a set of temporary symptoms such as visual disturbance, before the headache starts.

body.heading: How are they treated?
body.body:
For tension-type headache, the NHS says over-the-counter painkillers such as paracetamol and ibuprofen can help, along with relaxation, exercise and good sleep and posture habits. A GP may discuss a preventive medicine for frequent headaches.

For migraine, NICE advises that acute treatment is most effective when started early. It recommends a triptan combined with a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug or paracetamol, with the choice made by the clinician.

Taking painkillers or triptans too often can cause medication-overuse headache, so a GP can advise on how often is appropriate.

body.heading: When is a headache an emergency?
body.body:
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a sudden, extremely painful headache, a headache after a serious head injury, sudden problems with speech or memory, loss of vision, drowsiness or confusion, or a high temperature with other signs of meningitis such as a stiff neck or a rash.

These signs can mean a serious condition, and getting help promptly matters.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body:
A GP appointment is the route when headaches are frequent or severe, when painkillers are not helping, or when headaches affect work or daily life.

A GP can look for other causes, review any painkillers being taken and discuss preventive treatment where it is suitable. The site's page on headache sets out causes and warning signs in more detail.

NICE says it recommends Enhertu (trastuzumab deruxtecan) for adults with HER2-low advanced or metastatic breast cancer that has progressed after treatment. HER2 is a protein found on the surface of some breast cancer cells, and HER2-low describes cancers with a low level of it.

The recommendation appears in NICE's final draft guidance. NICE had earlier been unable to recommend the drug at the price the companies proposed.

NICE says a commercial solution has now been agreed. It followed changes to NICE's methods made as part of the UK/US Pharmaceutical Pricing Agreement.

nih-extra-year-school-dementia-diagnoses.summary: An NIH-funded study reports that one extra year of secondary school in the UK was linked to fewer dementia diagnoses later in life, with the largest effect in people at higher genetic risk.
keyPoints: An NIH news release dated 23 October 2026 describes an NIH-funded study of schooling and dementia.
The study used a UK reform that raised the minimum school-leaving age by one year.
It reports fewer dementia diagnoses later in life, with the largest effect among people at higher genetic risk.
This is research news from a US agency, not UK guidance.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
A US National Institutes of Health (NIH) news release dated 23 October 2026 describes a study that found an extra year of secondary school was associated with fewer dementia diagnoses later in life.

The NIH funded the study, which was led by researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and the University of Southern California.

The researchers analysed a UK education reform that raised the minimum school-leaving age by one year, treating it as a natural experiment.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
The release says the effect was largest among people at higher genetic risk of dementia.

The researchers estimated a reduction of 0.88 percentage points in Alzheimer's disease and related dementia over 50 years, which the release calls sizeable given how low overall dementia rates were in the study population.

The release notes that as the group ages, the gap between those who stayed in school and those who left may grow or shrink.

This is research news from a US agency; it does not change UK guidance.

numbness-and-tingling-causes-and-when-to.name: Numbness and tingling: causes and when to act
numbness-and-tingling-causes-and-when-to.headline: Numbness, tingling and pins and needles: common causes and when to get help
numbness-and-tingling-causes-and-when-to.summary: Pins and needles are usually brief and harmless, but numbness or tingling that lasts, keeps returning or comes with weakness needs checking. The NHS says to call 999 for sudden numbness on one side.
keyPoints: The NHS describes pins and needles as a pricking, tingling or numbing feeling, usually in the arms, hands, legs or feet.
Brief episodes often follow sitting or sleeping in one position, while longer-lasting symptoms can have other causes such as nerve damage or some medicines.
The NHS advises seeing a GP if pins and needles keep coming back or last a long time.
Sudden numbness or weakness down one side is a sign of stroke, and the NHS says to call 999.

body.heading: What are pins and needles?
body.body: The NHS describes pins and needles as a pricking, burning, tingling or numbing sensation. It usually affects the arms, hands, legs or feet. Brief spells are common after sitting or sleeping on a limb and usually pass.

body.heading: Why does it keep happening?
body.body: The NHS lists possible reasons for longer-lasting pins and needles, including a trapped nerve in the back or neck, nerve damage, poor diet and heavy drinking. Some treatments and substances are also listed, including chemotherapy, some medicines, lead and radiation. Conditions the NHS links to particular patterns include diabetes, Raynaud’s, hyperventilation, sciatica and multiple sclerosis.

body.heading: What is peripheral neuropathy?
body.body: Peripheral neuropathy is damage to the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord. Its main symptoms include numbness and tingling in the feet or hands, burning or stabbing pain, loss of balance and muscle weakness in the feet. Causes the NHS lists include diabetes, long-term heavy alcohol use, low vitamin B12 and an underactive thyroid. The NHS advises seeing a GP early if these symptoms appear, and blood tests may be arranged, especially for diabetes and vitamin B12 deficiency.

body.heading: What about the wrist and hand?
body.body: Carpal tunnel syndrome is pressure on a nerve in the wrist that causes tingling, numbness and pain in the hand and fingers. The symptoms are usually worse at night. The NHS says to see a GP if symptoms are getting worse or not going away, or if home treatment is not helping. When the diagnosis is unclear, a nerve conduction test or scans may be used.

body.heading: When is numbness an emergency?
body.body: The NHS lists sudden weakness or numbness down one side of the body among the symptoms of stroke. The NHS stroke test, FAST, stands for face, arms, speech and time to call 999. The NHS advises calling 999 even if the signs have stopped, and not driving yourself to A&E. A transient ischaemic attack (TIA) is a short-lived version of stroke symptoms, and the NHS says an assessment in hospital is still needed if the symptoms go away.

osteoarthritis-and-rheumatoid-arthritis-.name: Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis
osteoarthritis-and-rheumatoid-arthritis-.headline: Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis: how they differ
osteoarthritis-and-rheumatoid-arthritis-.summary: Osteoarthritis is wear in the joint cartilage; rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition that inflames the joint lining.
keyPoints: Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis in the UK and mostly affects the knees, hips and small joints of the hands.
Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the lining of the joints.
Rheumatoid arthritis usually affects joints on both sides of the body and brings long morning stiffness, as well as tiredness.
Osteoarthritis is managed with exercise, weight management and pain relief; rheumatoid arthritis needs medicines that reduce inflammation.
Early assessment matters for rheumatoid arthritis, so a GP appointment is the first step for persistent joint swelling or stiffness.

body.heading: What do the two conditions have in common?
body.body:
Both osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) are types of arthritis, and both cause joint pain and stiffness. Because of that overlap, people sometimes assume they are the same condition.

They are not. They have different causes, tend to affect different joints and are treated differently.

body.heading: What is osteoarthritis?
body.body:
Osteoarthritis is a condition that makes joints painful and stiff. The NHS says it is the most common type of arthritis in the UK.

The protective cartilage on the ends of the bones gradually breaks down. The NHS says the exact cause is not known, but several things are thought to raise the risk, and age is one of them.

It most often causes problems in the knees, hips and small joints of the hands. Symptoms can be mild and come and go, or be more constant and severe.

body.heading: What is rheumatoid arthritis?
body.body:
Rheumatoid arthritis is a long-term condition that causes pain, swelling and stiffness in the joints, usually in the hands, feet and wrists. It is an autoimmune disease: the immune system attacks the lining of the joints.

The NHS says it usually affects joints on both sides of the body, and that morning stiffness often lasts longer than it does in osteoarthritis. Some people also have tiredness, a fever or weight loss.

The trigger is not clear, but a higher risk is linked with being female, having a family history of the condition and smoking.

body.heading: How are they treated?
body.body:
For osteoarthritis, the NHS recommends regular exercise, keeping to a healthy weight, suitable footwear and aids that reduce strain on the joint. More severe symptoms may need painkillers and a structured exercise plan with a physiotherapist.

Surgery to repair, strengthen or replace a damaged joint is considered in some cases where other treatments have not helped.

Rheumatoid arthritis is treated with medicines that slow the disease and reduce inflammation, known as disease-modifying drugs, sometimes alongside biological treatments. Painkillers and steroids can ease symptoms, and physiotherapy and occupational therapy are part of care. With treatment it is possible to reduce the number of flares and limit long-term joint damage.

body.heading: How are they diagnosed?
body.body:
A GP asks about symptoms and examines the joints. Osteoarthritis can often be diagnosed from the symptoms and an examination.

For suspected rheumatoid arthritis, blood tests that look for inflammation are used, and the site's pages on CRP and ESR explain two of them. The laboratory report shows the reference range used. Imaging such as X-rays or ultrasound may also be arranged.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body:
A GP appointment is the usual route for joint pain, swelling or stiffness that does not settle. The NHS emphasises that early diagnosis and treatment of rheumatoid arthritis can help to prevent joint damage.

If a joint becomes suddenly hot, red and very painful, or there is a fever with a painful joint, the person should contact NHS 111 or the GP the same day. Severe symptoms such as sudden inability to move a limb need 999.

pelvic-pain-in-women-causes-and-when-to-.name: Pelvic pain in women: causes and when to act
pelvic-pain-in-women-causes-and-when-to-.headline: Pelvic pain in women: common causes, red flags and which NHS route to use
pelvic-pain-in-women-causes-and-when-to-.summary: Pelvic pain in women often comes from period pain, ovarian cysts or endometriosis, but a few causes are serious. The NHS says to call 999 for severe or worsening pain.
keyPoints: The NHS lists period pain, ovarian cysts, endometriosis and pregnancy-related pain among the common causes of pelvic pain in women.
Rarer causes include ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease and womb or ovarian cancer.
The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if the pain is severe, getting worse, or hurts when you move or touch the area.
Pain that comes and goes or does not go away is a reason for a routine GP appointment.

body.heading: What causes pelvic pain?
body.body: The NHS says pelvic pain is more common in women. Common causes include period pain, an ovarian cyst, endometriosis and pain related to pregnancy. Rarer but more serious causes include ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease, womb cancer and ovarian cancer.

body.heading: What is pelvic inflammatory disease?
body.body: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an infection of the female reproductive organs. Most cases start with a sexually transmitted infection such as chlamydia or gonorrhoea. Bacteria that normally live in the vagina cause some cases.

body.heading: When is a routine GP appointment appropriate?
body.body: The NHS suggests booking a GP appointment if pelvic pain comes and goes or does not go away. Bloating that does not go away, weight loss or changes in bowel habit are further reasons. Pain during sex, pain when peeing or pooing, and bleeding between periods are also listed.

body.heading: When should you call NHS 111 or an urgent GP?
body.body: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for pelvic pain with difficulty peeing or pooing, blood in urine or stool, unusual vaginal discharge or bleeding, or a very high temperature. The same advice applies if the person is or may be pregnant. For an ovarian cyst, sudden severe pelvic pain is a reason for an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

body.heading: When is it an emergency?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if pelvic pain is severe, getting worse, or hurts when you move or touch the area. Fainting or feeling dizzy, pain at the tip of the shoulder, difficulty breathing, heavy vaginal bleeding and sudden confusion are also on the 999 list. For PID, the NHS says to call 999 or go straight to A&E for severe pelvic pain or heavy vaginal bleeding, and not to drive yourself.

body.heading: Which tests might follow?
body.body: Assessment usually starts with questions and an examination. Urine or swab samples, a pregnancy test, and an ultrasound scan, which may be transvaginal, can follow, and an MRI scan of the pelvis is sometimes used. There is no single test for PID, and it is diagnosed from symptoms and an examination.

physical-activity-guidelines-adults.name: How much exercise adults need each week
physical-activity-guidelines-adults.summary: The NHS says adults aged 19 to 64 should do at least 150 minutes of moderate activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week, plus strength work.
keyPoints: The NHS lists at least 150 minutes of moderate activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week for adults aged 19 to 64.
Strengthening activities for the major muscle groups on at least two days a week are in addition to the aerobic minutes.
The NHS talk test separates moderate activity, where a person can talk but not sing, from vigorous activity, where only a few words fit between breaths.
The guidance also advises reducing long periods of sitting, and the 2019 update dropped the older rule that activity must come in bouts of at least ten minutes.

body.heading: How much activity do adults aged 19 to 64 need?
body.body: The NHS says adults aged 19 to 64 should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity activity a week, or 75 minutes of vigorous intensity activity a week. It also describes a mix of moderate and vigorous activity as a way of reaching the target. The NHS adds that 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week can give similar health benefits to 150 minutes of moderate activity. The guidance says activity should be spread across the week, and that all adults should aim to be active every day.

body.heading: What counts as moderate or vigorous?
body.body: The NHS uses a talk test: at moderate intensity a person can still talk but not sing. Brisk walking, cycling, dancing, water aerobics and pushing a lawn mower are listed as moderate activities. At vigorous intensity breathing becomes hard and fast, and a person cannot say more than a few words without pausing for breath. Running, swimming, fast or uphill cycling, skipping and team sports are listed as vigorous activities. The UK Chief Medical Officers' guidelines say very vigorous activity, such as sprinting or stair climbing, can count too, in shorter periods or mixed with other intensities.

body.heading: What are strengthening activities?
body.body: The NHS says adults should do strengthening activities on at least two days a week, working all the major muscle groups: legs, hips, back, abdomen, chest, shoulders and arms. Lifting weights, push-ups, sit-ups, heavy gardening such as digging and carrying heavy shopping are given as examples, along with yoga, pilates and tai chi. The NHS says these sessions are needed in addition to the aerobic minutes, because they do not count toward the 150 minutes. The Chief Medical Officers' guidance adds that any strengthening activity is better than none.

body.heading: Does sitting still matter?
body.body: The NHS guidance advises reducing the time spent sitting or lying down, and breaking up long periods of not moving with some activity. The Chief Medical Officers' guidance says adults should aim to minimise time spent sitting and, where possible, break up long inactive periods with at least light activity.

body.heading: What do the guidelines say about benefits and short bouts?
body.body: The NHS says exercising even once or twice a week can reduce the risk of heart disease or stroke. The 2019 revision of the UK guidelines removed the earlier rule that activity must come in bouts of at least ten minutes. The guidance says there is no minimum amount of physical activity needed for some health benefit.

body.heading: What does regular activity do for health?
body.body: The NHS says regular activity lowers the risk of conditions including heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression and dementia. It also says activity can improve self-esteem, mood, sleep quality and energy.

body.heading: What changes for adults aged 65 and over?
body.body: NHS guidance for older adults advises being active every day, even lightly. It recommends activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least two days a week, and 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week, built up gradually from current levels. The NHS advises speaking to a GP first for anyone who has not exercised for some time or who has medical conditions or concerns.

sepsis-warning-signs-and-what-to-do.name: Sepsis: warning signs and when to act
sepsis-warning-signs-and-what-to-do.headline: Sepsis: the warning signs in adults and children and when to call 999
sepsis-warning-signs-and-what-to-do.summary: Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to an infection; the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if sepsis is suspected.
keyPoints: Sepsis is a medical emergency that can follow an infection such as pneumonia, a urinary tract infection or cellulitis.
Signs in adults include confusion or slurred speech, uncontrollable shivering, muscle pain, difficulty breathing and blue, pale or blotchy skin.
Signs in babies and children include fast or difficult breathing, a fit, mottled or pale skin, and a rash that does not fade under pressure.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if someone may have sepsis, and not to drive there.
Treatment is in hospital and includes antibiotics, oxygen and fluids into a vein.

body.heading: What is sepsis?
body.body:
Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to an infection. The NHS describes it as a medical emergency.

It can happen after a bacterial infection such as pneumonia, a urinary tract infection or cellulitis. The exact cause is not always clear.

body.heading: What are the signs in adults?
body.body:
The NHS lists confusion or slurred speech, uncontrollable shivering, muscle pain, difficulty breathing, and blue, pale, grey or blotchy skin. Not passing urine for a long period is another sign.

A high temperature is less common in older adults, so a person can have sepsis without a fever.

body.heading: What are the signs in babies and children?
body.body:
The NHS lists fast or difficult breathing, a fit (seizure), mottled, bluish or pale skin, a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it, and being unusually sleepy or hard to wake.

In young children, refusing feeds or repeated vomiting can also be signs.

body.heading: Who is at higher risk?
body.body:
Sepsis mostly affects very young children, older adults and people with underlying health conditions. It can sometimes occur in people who are otherwise fit and healthy.

People with weakened immune systems, including those on long-term steroids or other medicines that suppress the immune system, are also at higher risk.

body.heading: When should someone call 999?
body.body:
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if an adult or child shows signs of sepsis, or if there is a worry that it could be sepsis. It advises asking someone to drive, or calling for an ambulance, rather than driving oneself.

Some local NHS guidance gives a middle route for less certain cases: an urgent GP or urgent treatment centre visit, or NHS 111. If the person seems seriously unwell, the safe route is 999.

body.heading: How is sepsis treated, and what happens afterwards?
body.body:
Sepsis is treated in hospital. Treatment includes antibiotics, oxygen to help with breathing, and fluids given into a vein. Some people need intensive care.

Recovery can take weeks or months. Some people have longer-lasting problems after sepsis, such as tiredness and changes in mood, which is sometimes called post-sepsis syndrome.

sleep-problems-what-helps.name: Sleep problems: what helps and when to get help
sleep-problems-what-helps.summary: The NHS says insomnia usually improves by changing sleeping habits, and that a GP can arrange CBT when habits alone do not help.
keyPoints: The NHS describes insomnia as regular difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early.
A steady bedtime and wake time, a dark, quiet room and winding down without screens are the habits the NHS pages describe most often.
The NHS suggests seeing a GP if changing habits has not helped, or if sleep trouble has lasted for months.
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the main treatment described by NHS sources; sleeping pills are rarely prescribed.

body.heading: What counts as insomnia?
body.body:
The NHS says a person who regularly finds it hard to fall asleep, stay asleep or wake up too early may have insomnia. It also says insomnia usually gets better by changing sleeping habits.

A primary care pathway from NHS South Yorkshire says insomnia often starts with a specific problem or a change in life circumstances. The same pathway lists physical conditions such as sleep apnoea as able to make insomnia worse. It also suggests that a clinician asks whether a medicine could be a cause, and considers anxiety or depression as possible underlying factors.

body.heading: Which sleep habits do NHS pages describe?
body.body:
The NHS Every Mind Matters pages say a regular sleep routine can make it easier to fall asleep, because going to bed and getting up at similar times each day helps the body know when it is time to sleep. They suggest keeping the same routine on days off. They also suggest keeping phones, tablets and computers away for an hour before bed, because the light can delay sleep. Reading, meditation or breathing exercises are given as alternatives.

A dark, quiet and cool bedroom is a recurring recommendation across NHS pages. NHS pages also advise against caffeine, smoking and alcohol in the hours before bed, although the exact timing differs from page to page. Some pages advise against napping during the day and describe regular daytime exercise as helpful. For someone who worries in bed, the NHS suggests writing a list of tasks for the next day before going to sleep.

body.heading: What does the NHS suggest when sleep will not come?
body.body: If a person is still awake after about 20 minutes, the NHS suggests getting up, doing something relaxing in another room, and going back to bed when sleepy.

body.heading: When does the NHS suggest seeing a GP?
body.body: The NHS suggests seeing a GP if changing sleeping habits has not helped insomnia, or if there has been trouble sleeping for months. A GP may refer a person for cognitive behavioural therapy, or CBT, which helps change the thoughts and behaviours that get in the way of sleep. The NHS says GPs now rarely prescribe sleeping pills for insomnia, because they can have serious side effects and a person can become dependent on them.

body.heading: What does CBT for insomnia involve?
body.body: NHS sources describe cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, known as CBT-I, as the main treatment for long-term insomnia. A University College London Hospitals service says most patients with insomnia are offered a course of CBT-I first, and that waiting lists can apply. A Scottish NHS self-help guide describes Sleepio as a free digital treatment that delivers a six-week CBT-I programme. A primary care guideline from Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire and Berkshire West advises that medicines are best avoided in the long-term management of insomnia.

body.heading: How much sleep do adults need, and why does it matter?
body.body: NHS sources put the amount most adults need at about 7 to 9 hours a night. One NHS page says age, health and daily routine can all affect how much sleep a person needs. NHS Every Mind Matters says getting enough sleep can support mood, energy, the immune system and overall health. A United States guide from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute adds that regularly getting too little or very poor quality sleep increases the risk of high blood pressure, heart disease and other health problems. NHS pages list feeling very tired, irritable or sleepy during the day among the signs of not sleeping enough.

body.heading: Could another sleep disorder be involved?
body.body: The NHS says a person may be referred to a sleep clinic if they have symptoms of another sleep disorder, such as sleep apnoea. Fatigue, meaning overwhelming tiredness that rest and sleep do not relieve, may point to an underlying medical condition, according to NHS guidance linked to NHS Lothian.

statins-common-questions-answered.name: Statins: common questions answered
statins-common-questions-answered.headline: Statins: what they do and the common concerns, as the NHS describes them
statins-common-questions-answered.summary: The NHS says statins lower the cholesterol the body makes, to reduce the risk of heart attacks and strokes, and they are usually taken long term.
keyPoints: Statins work by lowering the amount of cholesterol the body makes, which helps stop cholesterol building up in blood vessels.
The NHS says statins may be offered to people at higher risk of cardiovascular disease and to people who already have it.
Statins are usually taken long term, and the NHS says stopping can let cholesterol rise again.
Muscle pain, tenderness, weakness or cramps with no clear cause is something the NHS says to get medical advice about.
Grapefruit juice affects some statins more than others, so the NHS says to ask a pharmacist or GP about the one prescribed.
The NHS says that stopping a statin can let cholesterol rise again, so it advises talking to a doctor first.

body.heading: What do statins do?
body.body:
Statins are medicines that lower cholesterol.

Cholesterol is a fatty substance made by the liver and carried in the blood.

According to the NHS, statins reduce how much cholesterol the body makes. This helps prevent a build-up of cholesterol in the blood vessels. High cholesterol can lead to cardiovascular disease, which includes heart attacks, strokes and peripheral arterial disease.

Atorvastatin and rosuvastatin are two of the statins the NHS describes, along with others such as simvastatin and pravastatin.

body.heading: Who are statins for?
body.body:
The NHS says statins may be offered to people at higher risk of cardiovascular disease when healthy lifestyle changes have not helped or are unlikely to help on their own. They may also be offered to people who already have cardiovascular disease, to lower the risk of a heart attack or stroke.

NICE has published a patient decision aid, "Are statins the best choice for me?", for people weighing up whether statins are right for them.

The NHS says most adults can take atorvastatin, and that it is sometimes prescribed for children aged 10 and over. Caution is needed for people with liver or kidney problems or a past allergic reaction to a statin. The NHS advises against atorvastatin in pregnancy.

body.heading: How long are statins taken for?
body.body:
The NHS says statins are usually taken long term.

For atorvastatin, the NHS says it can be taken for many years and works best when taken for a long time. It says cholesterol should fall within about four weeks if the medicine is taken as prescribed.

The NHS advises continuing atorvastatin even when a person feels well.

body.heading: What side effects can statins cause?
body.body:
For atorvastatin, the NHS lists headaches, dizziness, nausea, muscle aches and digestive upset such as diarrhoea or indigestion as common side effects.

For rosuvastatin, the NHS says side effects often ease as the body gets used to the medicine, and that serious ones are rare.

The NHS lists rare serious effects including liver inflammation, pancreatitis, muscle damage and allergic reactions. It says yellowing of the skin or eyes can be a sign of liver problems, and that prompt medical attention is needed. For rosuvastatin, severe breathing or swallowing problems, or sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, are emergencies for which the NHS says to call 999.

For rosuvastatin, the NHS says to contact a doctor if side effects last more than a few days or get worse.

body.heading: What about muscle pain?
body.body:
The NHS lists muscle pain, tenderness, weakness or cramps with no clear cause as possible signs of muscle damage. For rosuvastatin it says to get medical advice promptly if these happen.

For atorvastatin, the NHS advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111 straight away for these symptoms. The NHS says that if side effects are the reason someone wants to stop, the doctor may be able to change the dose or switch medicine.

body.heading: Do grapefruit juice and other things affect statins?
body.body:
The NHS says grapefruit and grapefruit juice can affect some medicines by raising the level of the medicine in the blood, which makes side effects more likely.

The NHS treats statins differently: grapefruit juice is a particular concern with simvastatin, while atorvastatin is affected mainly by large amounts and some other statins are generally not a concern.

The NHS also says drinking a lot of alcohol regularly increases the chance of side effects and liver problems with atorvastatin.

It advises talking to a GP or pharmacist about grapefruit if it is a regular part of the diet and a medicine that is affected has been prescribed.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about stopping a statin?
body.body:
The NHS says stopping atorvastatin may cause cholesterol to rise, which increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

It says there are no withdrawal symptoms and no evidence that atorvastatin is addictive.

For rosuvastatin, the NHS advises talking to a doctor before stopping because of side effects, since the problem may be unrelated to the medicine. The NHS also advises not stopping a medicine without advice.

stop-smoking-nhs-support.name: Stopping smoking: the support the NHS offers
stop-smoking-nhs-support.summary: NHS stop smoking services offer nicotine replacement, medicines and professional support, and people in England can self-refer through NHS Better Health.
keyPoints: NHS stop smoking services provide nicotine replacement therapy and prescription medicines, together with professional support in the first months after quitting.
Vapes are not available as medicines on the NHS, though some local services may offer a free starter pack.
The NHS says cravings are short-lived and that withdrawal symptoms are temporary.
NHS Better Health also offers a personal quit plan and the NHS Quit Smoking app.

body.heading: What help do NHS stop smoking services provide?
body.body: NHS stop smoking services offer information and advice and professional support during the first few months after someone stops smoking. They provide nicotine replacement therapy, such as patches and gum, and medicines such as varenicline and bupropion. In England people can refer themselves to a local service through the NHS Better Health website, and can also speak to a GP. Availability and arrangements differ between the four UK nations and between areas.

body.heading: How do nicotine replacement and medicines work?
body.body: Nicotine replacement therapy comes as patches, gum, lozenges, inhalators and mouth or nasal sprays. The NHS describes it as safe, proven to work and able to double the chances of quitting for good. Varenicline works by blocking the effects of nicotine in the brain, which makes smoking less enjoyable and helps with withdrawal symptoms. NHS pages say that a nicotine-free medicine such as varenicline or cytisine can be combined with a nicotine product, and describe the combination as giving the best chance of success.

body.heading: Where do vapes fit in?
body.body: E-cigarettes are not currently available as medicines, so stop smoking services cannot supply them and they cannot be prescribed on the NHS. Some local stop smoking services may still offer a free starter pack.

body.heading: What happens in the body after stopping?
body.body: The NHS sets out a timeline: within about 20 minutes the pulse rate begins to return to normal. By 48 hours carbon monoxide levels in the blood have fallen to those of a non-smoker. After one year the risk of a heart attack is about half that of a person who smokes, and after ten years the risk of dying from lung cancer is about half. NHS pages also report mental health benefits: once the withdrawal stage has passed, people report less anxiety, depression and stress.

body.heading: What are cravings and withdrawal like?
body.body: Withdrawal symptoms are temporary, and the NHS lists feeling on edge or anxious and wanting a cigarette among them. NHS inform, the Scottish NHS site, says cravings improve after the first two to three weeks and that most withdrawal symptoms fade by about two weeks. The NHS says an individual craving lasts only a short time. Walking, chewing sugar-free gum and deep breathing are among the coping ideas it lists.

body.heading: What other support is available?
body.body: NHS Better Health offers a free personalised quit plan and the NHS Quit Smoking app. In 2024 NHS England announced that the stop smoking medicine cytisine was being rolled out to help people quit.

body.heading: Why does the NHS stress stopping?
body.body: The NHS Better Health site says the harm from smoking reaches beyond the lungs, including hearing and vision loss, dementia risk, joint damage and digestive problems. It says smoking damages blood vessels and narrows arteries, and strains the heart by raising blood pressure. The NHS also says smoking increases the risk of developing more than 50 serious health conditions. The relief a cigarette seems to give from stress is short-lived, and smoking can make anxiety and low mood worse over time, according to the NHS. Babies and children living with smoke face a higher risk of chest infections, meningitis and worsening asthma, the NHS says.

stress-symptoms-and-getting-help.name: Stress: how it shows up and where to get help
stress-symptoms-and-getting-help.summary: Stress is a reaction to mental or emotional pressure that can affect mood, body and behaviour; the NHS suggests a GP or NHS 111 when it affects daily life.
keyPoints: The NHS describes stress as usually a reaction to mental or emotional pressure, often linked to feeling a loss of control.
Stress can show up as emotional changes, physical symptoms such as headaches and stomach problems, and changes in behaviour.
Long-term or severe stress can lead to exhaustion of body, mind and emotions, often called burnout.
Adults in England can refer themselves to NHS Talking Therapies without seeing a GP.

body.heading: What is stress?
body.body: The NHS describes stress as usually a reaction to mental or emotional pressure, often related to feeling a loss of control over something, though sometimes there is no obvious cause. Common triggers it lists include pressure at work, relationship or family difficulties, money worries, illness and bereavement. Stress can be useful in small doses, but the NHS says it can become a problem when it is constant. Long-term or severe stress can lead to physical, mental and emotional exhaustion, often called burnout.

body.heading: How does stress show up in the body and behaviour?
body.body: The NHS says stress can affect emotions, causing irritability, anger, tearfulness, worry and feeling overwhelmed. Physical symptoms listed include stomach problems, stress headaches, muscle pain, rashes and dizziness. The NHS also says stress can raise blood pressure or cause chest pains, which should ease once the stress does. Behaviour can change too, with sleeping too much or too little, eating more or less, avoiding people or places, or drinking or smoking more.

body.heading: What does the NHS suggest for managing stress?
body.body: NHS pages suggest identifying the cause as the first step, then breaking large tasks into small targets and focusing on what can be changed. Controlled breathing, deep muscle relaxation and mindful breathing are listed as ways to reduce tension and some of the physical signs of stress. Talking to trusted friends, family or colleagues, or contacting a helpline, is also suggested. Short CBT-based videos and guides are offered to work through problems in new ways and build resilience. The NHS advises against using alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to relieve stress, because these can contribute to poor mental health.

body.heading: When does the NHS suggest getting help?
body.body: If stress is affecting daily life, the NHS suggests contacting NHS 111 or talking to a GP. In England, adults aged 18 and over can refer themselves directly to NHS Talking Therapies without seeing a GP, and in some areas the minimum age is 16. If stress has led to thoughts of self-harm or suicide, call 999 if there is immediate danger, use NHS 111 and choose the mental health option for urgent help, or contact Samaritans free at any time on 116 123.

body.heading: What happens in the body during stress?
body.body: An NHS self-help guide describes stress as the body's reaction to feeling under threat, known as the fight or flight response, and says a certain amount of pressure can be helpful and motivating. The British Heart Foundation explains that the brain signals the body to release hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol. It says that if this response keeps being switched on again and again, over time it can take its toll on the body. The NHS guide says stress that continues and is not managed can be bad for health.

stroke-and-tia-spotting-the-signs.name: Stroke and TIA: spotting the signs
stroke-and-tia-spotting-the-signs.headline: Stroke and TIA: spotting the signs and why 999 is the route
stroke-and-tia-spotting-the-signs.summary: A stroke and a TIA cause the same symptoms; in a TIA they pass, but both are emergencies and the NHS says to call 999.
keyPoints: The FAST test checks for face drooping, arm weakness and speech problems, and the NHS says to call 999 if any sign is present.
A TIA, sometimes called a mini-stroke, causes the same symptoms as a stroke but they go away, usually within a short time.
A TIA is a warning that a full stroke may follow, so it needs urgent assessment even when symptoms have settled.
Treatment differs for strokes caused by a blood clot and strokes caused by bleeding, which is why a hospital scan comes first.
The Stroke Association runs a support helpline for people affected by stroke.

body.heading: What are the signs of a stroke?
body.body:
The FAST test is used across the UK to spot a stroke. It checks the face, the arms and the speech: does the face droop on one side, can the person raise both arms, and is speech slurred or confused.

The NHS and the Stroke Association say that any one of these signs is a reason to call 999. It is the time, not the cause, that matters most in treatment.

body.heading: What is a TIA, and how does it differ from a stroke?
body.body:
A transient ischaemic attack, or TIA, is often called a mini-stroke. It causes the same symptoms as a stroke, but they are temporary.

The Stroke Association says the symptoms of a TIA usually last from a few minutes to a few hours and settle completely within 24 hours. If symptoms last longer than that, it is classed as a stroke.

In the first minutes it is usually impossible to tell the two apart, so both are treated as emergencies.

body.heading: Why does a TIA matter if the symptoms pass?
body.body:
A TIA can be a warning sign that a full stroke may follow. The Stroke Association says the risk is greatest in the first days and weeks afterwards.

For this reason the NHS says a suspected TIA should be assessed urgently, even if the symptoms have gone by the time the ambulance arrives. A person whose symptoms have cleared still needs to be seen in hospital.

body.heading: What happens in hospital?
body.body:
A scan is used to find out whether a stroke is caused by a blood clot (ischaemic) or by bleeding in the brain (haemorrhagic), because the treatments differ.

For an ischaemic stroke, emergency options include clot-busting medicine, called thrombolysis, and removal of the clot with a catheter, called thrombectomy. A stroke caused by bleeding is treated differently, for example by lowering blood pressure.

These treatments work best when started early, which is part of why calling 999 matters.

body.heading: How is a suspected TIA treated?
body.body:
For a suspected TIA, the NHS says aspirin is usually given to lower the risk of a stroke, unless there is a medical reason to avoid it. The person is then referred to a specialist doctor or nurse within 24 hours of the symptoms.

Longer-term care focuses on preventing clots and tackling the risks behind them, such as high blood pressure. Medicines that thin the blood or reduce clotting may be used, and sometimes surgery is offered to clear a narrowed artery in the neck.

body.heading: Where can people find support?
body.body:
The Stroke Association runs a Stroke Support Helpline on 0303 3033 100 for people affected by stroke and TIA, and for their families.

A GP can explain what the diagnosis means and arrange follow-up care. In an emergency, the route is always 999.

swollen-ankles-and-legs-causes-and-red-f.name: Swollen ankles and legs: causes and red flags
swollen-ankles-and-legs-causes-and-red-f.headline: Swollen ankles, feet and legs: common causes and when to get help
swollen-ankles-and-legs-causes-and-red-f.summary: Swollen ankles and legs often come from sitting or standing for long periods, but can signal a clot or a heart, kidney or liver problem. The NHS names the signs that need 111 or 999.
keyPoints: The NHS lists sitting or standing for long periods, a high-salt diet, being overweight, pregnancy and some medicines among the more common causes of swollen ankles and legs.
Less often, swelling comes from a blood clot, an infection, or a heart, kidney or liver problem.
The NHS advises seeing a GP if swelling in both legs does not improve after a few days of home care, gets worse, or occurs in someone with a heart, kidney or leg vein condition.
Breathlessness, chest pain, coughing up blood or feeling faint with leg swelling may mean a clot in the lungs, which needs a 999 call.

body.heading: What commonly causes swollen ankles?
body.body: The NHS calls swollen ankles, feet and legs oedema, which is a build-up of fluid in the body’s tissues. The NHS lists sitting or standing still for long periods, a high-salt diet and being overweight as lifestyle factors. Pregnancy, varicose veins and thyroid problems can also cause swelling. Some medicines are listed too, including certain blood pressure medicines, contraceptive pills, hormone therapy, antidepressants and steroids.

body.heading: What are the less common causes?
body.body: Less commonly, swelling can follow an injury or an insect bite, or come from a blood clot or an infection. The NHS also lists problems with the heart, kidneys or liver as causes. The British Heart Foundation adds lymphoedema, a problem with the drainage of lymph fluid, as another cause.

body.heading: Why does one swollen leg matter more?
body.body: NHS 111 Wales advises seeking advice for swelling in only one leg when there is no known cause. The NHS describes deep vein thrombosis (DVT) as throbbing pain in one leg, usually in the calf or thigh, with swelling in that leg. The skin over a DVT can look red, blue or darker than usual.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP if swelling in both legs has not improved after a few days of home care, if it gets worse, or if it occurs in someone with a heart, kidney or leg vein condition.

body.heading: Which signs mean urgent help?
body.body: NHS 111 Wales advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for swelling that is severe, painful, sudden, red or hot, or that comes with a high temperature or shivering. The same page lists swelling in the feet, ankles or legs of a person with diabetes as a reason for urgent advice. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if leg swelling comes with shortness of breath or chest pain, because a clot can travel to the lungs. Coughing up blood or feeling faint are also described as symptoms of a clot in the lungs. In pregnancy, very severe swelling of the hands, face or ankles with nausea can be a sign of pre-eclampsia, and NHS inform says to contact a midwife or GP straight away.

tiredness-and-fatigue-causes-and-gp-chec.name: Tiredness and fatigue: causes and next steps
tiredness-and-fatigue-causes-and-gp-chec.headline: Tiredness that will not go away: common causes and what a GP checks
tiredness-and-fatigue-causes-and-gp-chec.summary: Tiredness is common and often has an ordinary cause such as poor sleep, stress or illness. The NHS advises a GP appointment when it lasts a few weeks without explanation.
keyPoints: The NHS lists poor sleep, an unhealthy lifestyle, hormonal changes, some illnesses and some medicines among the common causes of tiredness.
The NHS advises booking a GP appointment when tiredness has lasted a few weeks without a clear reason, affects daily life or comes with other symptoms such as weight loss.
A GP may arrange blood tests to look for conditions such as anaemia, diabetes or an overactive thyroid.
Self-help advice from the NHS covers diet, exercise, relaxation and sleep habits.

body.heading: What counts as fatigue?
body.body: Everyone feels tired from time to time, and the NHS treats tiredness as a common symptom with many possible causes. Fatigue is described by NHS 111 Wales as an overwhelming tiredness that is not relieved by rest and sleep. If there is no obvious reason for the tiredness and it goes on for a while without improving, the NHS says it may be a sign of a medical condition.

body.heading: What are the common causes?
body.body: The NHS names poor sleep or difficulty getting to sleep (insomnia) and an unhealthy lifestyle as common causes. Hormonal changes, such as those of puberty, pregnancy or the menopause, can also make people tired. Stress, depression and bereavement are also listed as triggers. Some medicines, including chemotherapy, can cause tiredness. Among medical conditions, the NHS mentions sleep apnoea, iron deficiency anaemia, diabetes and an overactive thyroid as possible reasons. Gasping, snorting or choking noises during sleep are one of the reasons the NHS gives for seeing a GP, because they can point to a sleep problem.

body.heading: When is it worth seeing a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises a routine GP appointment if tiredness has lasted a few weeks and the cause is unclear. A GP appointment is also advised if the tiredness affects daily life. Other symptoms alongside the tiredness, such as weight loss or changes in mood, are further reasons to book one. The NHS page also advises against trying to diagnose the cause yourself, and suggests seeing a GP if you are worried.

body.heading: What might a GP do?
body.body: A GP will usually ask about lifestyle and general health to look for an explanation. The NHS says tests may be needed, such as blood tests to check for anaemia, diabetes or an overactive thyroid. If the cause is still unclear, a GP may refer the person to a specialist.

body.heading: What does the NHS suggest for self-care?
body.body: The NHS self-help advice covers eating a healthy diet, taking exercise, finding ways to relax and improving sleep. Caffeine can disrupt sleep, which is one reason it appears in the NHS tips. The NHS also says there is some evidence that talking therapies such as counselling or cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) may help with fatigue, and a GP can arrange a referral.

body.heading: Could it be ME/CFS?
body.body: Myalgic encephalomyelitis or chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) is a long-term condition whose most common symptom is extreme tiredness. There is no specific test for ME/CFS, so a diagnosis is made from the symptoms and by ruling out other conditions that could explain them.

type-1-and-type-2-diabetes-compared.name: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes compared
type-1-and-type-2-diabetes-compared.headline: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes compared: causes, symptoms and treatment
type-1-and-type-2-diabetes-compared.summary: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition treated with insulin; type 2 develops when the body makes too little insulin or it works poorly.
keyPoints: In type 1 diabetes the immune system destroys the cells that make insulin, so the body makes little or no insulin.
In type 2 diabetes the body makes too little insulin or the insulin it makes does not work well.
Type 1 usually develops over days to weeks, while type 2 usually develops gradually over years.
Type 1 is treated with insulin, with blood glucose monitoring; type 2 is usually managed first with diet, activity and weight management.
Neither type has a permanent cure, although type 2 can sometimes be put into remission.

body.heading: What do the two types have in common?
body.body:
Diabetes is a condition in which there is too much glucose, a type of sugar, in the blood. Both type 1 and type 2 involve insulin, the hormone that helps glucose move out of the blood and into the body's cells.

The two types share several symptoms: increased thirst, passing urine more often, tiredness and weight loss. The difference lies in why the problem arises and how it is managed.

body.heading: What causes type 1 diabetes?
body.body:
Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition. The immune system destroys the cells in the pancreas that make insulin, so the body makes little or no insulin.

It usually develops over days to weeks, particularly in children. In adults it can take a few months to appear.

body.heading: What causes type 2 diabetes?
body.body:
Type 2 diabetes is not an autoimmune condition. Either the body does not make enough insulin, or the insulin it makes does not work as well as it should.

Diabetes UK lists age, family history, ethnicity and weight among the risk factors.

Type 2 usually develops gradually over years, and it is often picked up at a routine check-up rather than because of obvious symptoms.

body.heading: How are the two types treated?
body.body:
Type 1 diabetes is treated with insulin, which is needed for life, alongside monitoring of blood glucose.

Type 2 diabetes is usually managed first through diet, physical activity and weight management. Medicine may be added if needed, such as metformin, and some people also need insulin.

The clinician looking after the person decides which treatment is right, and the plan can change over time.

body.heading: Can diabetes be cured?
body.body:
Diabetes UK says neither type currently has a permanent cure. Type 2 diabetes can sometimes be put into remission, and it can sometimes be prevented.

Remission does not mean the condition has gone for good, which is why regular checks are still part of care.

body.heading: How is diabetes checked, and who should be seen?
body.body:
Blood tests are used to diagnose and monitor diabetes. The site's pages on blood glucose and on HbA1c explain what they show, and the laboratory report shows the reference range used.

A GP appointment is the route for anyone who has the symptoms above, or who is worried about their risk of type 2 diabetes. The NHS website sets out the symptoms to look for.

underactive-and-overactive-thyroid-compa.name: Underactive and overactive thyroid
underactive-and-overactive-thyroid-compa.headline: Underactive and overactive thyroid compared: symptoms, causes and treatment
underactive-and-overactive-thyroid-compa.summary: An underactive thyroid makes too little hormone and slows the body down; an overactive thyroid makes too much and speeds it up.
keyPoints: An underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) means the gland does not make enough thyroid hormone; an overactive one (hyperthyroidism) means it makes too much.
Symptoms are broadly opposite: tiredness and feeling cold with an underactive thyroid, weight loss and feeling hot with an overactive one.
The main cause of an underactive thyroid in the UK is an autoimmune condition called Hashimoto's disease.
Underactive thyroid is usually treated with levothyroxine tablets; overactive thyroid with medicine, radioactive iodine or surgery.
Treatment for an overactive thyroid can lead to an underactive thyroid, so follow-up blood tests matter.

body.heading: What does the thyroid do?
body.body: The thyroid is a gland in the neck that makes hormones which help control the body's energy use. When it makes too little hormone the body's processes slow down, and when it makes too much they speed up.

body.heading: What are the symptoms of an underactive thyroid?
body.body:
The NHS describes an underactive thyroid as a common condition in which the thyroid does not make enough hormone. Typical symptoms are tiredness, feeling cold, weight gain, constipation, low mood, and dry skin or hair loss.

Symptoms may be mild and can develop slowly, so they are not always easy to notice.

body.heading: What are the symptoms of an overactive thyroid?
body.body:
The NHS says an overactive thyroid, also called hyperthyroidism, means the thyroid makes too much hormone. Symptoms include nervousness or irritability, difficulty sleeping, persistent tiredness, sensitivity to heat, and a fast or irregular heartbeat.

Weight loss despite a normal or increased appetite and a swelling in the neck, called a goitre, can also occur.

body.heading: What causes each condition?
body.body:
In the UK, the main cause of an underactive thyroid is Hashimoto's disease, an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the thyroid.

The main cause of an overactive thyroid is Graves' disease, another autoimmune condition. Thyroid nodules and some medicines can also cause it.

body.heading: How are they treated?
body.body:
An underactive thyroid is usually treated with levothyroxine tablets, which replace the missing hormone. The NHS says they are usually needed for life, with regular blood tests to check that the treatment is right.

An overactive thyroid can be treated with antithyroid medicine, radioactive iodine or surgery. Beta blockers can ease symptoms such as palpitations in the meantime.

Radioactive iodine often leads to an underactive thyroid that then needs lifelong hormone tablets.

body.heading: How is the thyroid tested, and when should someone get help?
body.body:
Thyroid function is checked with blood tests that measure thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and thyroid hormones. The site's pages on thyroid function tests and TSH explain them, and the laboratory report shows the reference range used.

A GP appointment is the route for symptoms that could be thyroid-related. The NHS advises calling 999 if a thyroid storm, a rare and life-threatening flare-up of an overactive thyroid, is suspected.

unexplained-weight-loss-causes-and-next-.name: Unexplained weight loss: causes and next steps
unexplained-weight-loss-causes-and-next-.headline: Losing weight without trying: possible causes and when to see a GP
unexplained-weight-loss-causes-and-next-.summary: Losing weight without changing diet or exercise has many causes, from stress to thyroid or digestive conditions. The NHS advises seeing a GP as a precaution.
keyPoints: Unintentional weight loss means losing weight without changing diet or exercise, and the NHS advises seeing a GP as a precaution.
The NHS lists mental health conditions, digestive problems, overactive thyroid and heart failure among the causes.
A GP will ask about general health and may arrange tests or scans.

body.heading: What is unintentional weight loss?
body.body: Unintentional weight loss is losing weight without changing your diet or exercise routine. The NHS treats it as a possible sign of stress or serious illness, and advises seeing a GP as a precaution.

body.heading: What can cause it?
body.body: Mental health conditions such as depression, anxiety, eating disorders and obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) are on the NHS list. Digestive problems are listed, including coeliac disease and inflammatory bowel disease. Hormone conditions such as an overactive thyroid and type 1 diabetes can cause weight loss. Heart conditions such as heart failure are also listed. Some medicines can cause weight loss as well, and cancer is another possible cause.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP if you keep losing weight without changing your diet or exercise. The NHS says to go as soon as possible if the weight loss comes with other symptoms. NHS malnutrition advice also says to see a GP after losing a lot of weight unintentionally over a few months.

body.heading: What happens at the appointment?
body.body: A GP will ask about general health and may arrange some tests or scans. Blood tests commonly used in the first assessment can include a full blood count, liver and kidney function, thyroid function and a test for diabetes.

uti-and-cystitis-what-they-are.name: UTI and cystitis: what they are
uti-and-cystitis-what-they-are.headline: Urinary tract infection and cystitis: symptoms, treatment and when to get help
uti-and-cystitis-what-they-are.summary: A urinary tract infection (UTI) can affect the bladder, urethra or kidneys; cystitis is a UTI of the bladder, and many cases are treated with antibiotics.
keyPoints: A urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection anywhere in the urinary system, and cystitis is a UTI in the bladder.
Common symptoms are pain or burning when passing urine, needing to go more often or urgently, and cloudy urine.
Fever, pain in the back or side below the ribs, or blood in the urine can point to a more serious infection.
Antibiotics are used for many UTIs, but the NHS says they are not always needed, and mild cases can settle on their own.
Urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP is advised for symptoms such as blood in the urine, back pain or a high temperature.

body.heading: What is the difference between a UTI and cystitis?
body.body:
A urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection in any part of the urinary system, which includes the kidneys, the tubes that carry urine, the bladder and the urethra. Cystitis is the name for an infection of the bladder.

The NHS describes UTIs as common, and many of them are cystitis.

body.heading: What are the symptoms?
body.body:
The NHS lists pain or burning when passing urine, needing to pass urine more often or more urgently than usual, and cloudy urine. Cystitis can also bring lower tummy pain.

A kidney infection is more serious. Symptoms that point towards it include a high temperature, pain in the back or side under the ribs, feeling shivery or unwell, and blood in the urine.

Older or frail people may show confusion or drowsiness rather than typical urinary symptoms.

body.heading: What causes a UTI?
body.body:
UTIs happen when bacteria, usually from the gut, get into the urinary tract. Pregnancy, using spermicide with contraception and not drinking enough fluids are among the things the NHS links with a higher chance of getting one.

People who use a urinary catheter, or who have a weakened immune system, are also at higher risk.

body.heading: How is a UTI treated?
body.body:
Mild cases can settle without antibiotics. The NHS says drinking plenty of fluids and taking a painkiller such as paracetamol can ease symptoms, and that there is no good evidence to support cranberry products.

A GP or pharmacist may offer antibiotics, usually a short course for cystitis. Sometimes the clinician may provide a prescription to be used only if symptoms do not improve. A urine sample can be tested, although this is not always needed.

Kidney infections are usually treated with a longer course of antibiotics, and some people need care in hospital.

body.heading: When should someone get medical help?
body.body:
The NHS advises contacting a GP or NHS 111 the same day for blood in the urine, pain in the back or side, a very high or low temperature, vomiting, or not having passed urine all day. The same applies to anyone who is pregnant, uses a catheter or has a weakened immune system.

A GP appointment is the route when symptoms have not cleared within a few days, after antibiotics, or when UTIs keep coming back.

Confusion, drowsiness or difficulty speaking can be a sign of a serious infection, and the route is 999 or A&E.

vitamin-d-and-supplements-who-needs-them.name: Vitamins and supplements: who may need them
vitamin-d-and-supplements-who-needs-them.summary: The NHS says most people can get what they need from a balanced diet, with vitamin D in autumn and winter and folic acid in early pregnancy as main exceptions.
keyPoints: NHS pages advise that everyone should consider a daily 10 microgram vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter, because it is hard to get enough from food alone.
Some groups, including people who are rarely outdoors and people with dark skin, are advised to take vitamin D all year.
The NHS advises anyone who is pregnant or could become pregnant to take a folic acid supplement until the twelfth week of pregnancy.
More is not always better: the NHS warns that very high vitamin D intakes could be harmful.

body.heading: Can a balanced diet provide everything?
body.body: NHS pages on vitamins and minerals describe getting what the body needs from a balanced diet, with supplements recommended only for some people and times of year. Vitamin D is the main example, because it is difficult for people to get enough from food alone.

body.heading: Who is advised to take vitamin D?
body.body: The NHS says everyone should consider a daily 10 microgram vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter. NHS England starts this seasonal advice at age 4, while NHS inform in Scotland starts it at age 5. Some groups are advised to take it all year: people who are not often outdoors, such as those who are frail or housebound or living in care homes, people who usually cover most of their skin outdoors, and people with dark skin from African, African-Caribbean or South Asian backgrounds. For breastfed babies the NHS advises a daily vitamin D supplement throughout the year, and children aged 1 to 4 are also advised to take it year-round. Healthy Start vitamin products are free for eligible families.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about pregnancy?
body.body: Anyone who is pregnant or could become pregnant is advised to take a 400 microgram folic acid supplement every day until the twelfth week of pregnancy. The NHS says some people need a higher dose, for example those with diabetes or taking medicine for epilepsy, and that this is arranged with a doctor.

body.heading: Can too much be harmful?
body.body: For vitamin D, the NHS says taking more than 100 micrograms a day could be harmful, and this applies to adults, pregnant and breastfeeding women and children aged 11 to 17. For folic acid, the NHS says too much could be harmful, but 1 milligram or less a day is unlikely to cause any harm.

body.heading: What do some common nutrients do?
body.body: The NHS guide to vitamins and minerals covers vitamins A, B, C, D, E and K, folic acid, calcium, iodine and iron. For vitamin A and for iron, the NHS says most people can get all they need from a varied and balanced diet. The NHS says vitamin D helps regulate the amount of calcium and phosphate in the body, and that sunlight is the main source. It says that from about late March or early April to the end of September most people can make all the vitamin D they need from sunlight on the skin. Iron is important for making red blood cells, which carry oxygen around the body. Liver is very rich in vitamin A, and the NHS says liver or liver products such as pâté should not be eaten more than once a week.
